subject: algo
name: Algorithms
tagline: A named technique for a recurring shape of problem
summary: An algorithm is a procedure with a cost. Interview problems repeat a small set of shapes, and naming the shape is most of the work: sorting, searching, two pointers, sliding window, greedy, dynamic programming and backtracking.

sections.heading: Recognise the shape before you code
body: Almost every problem is one of a handful of shapes. Sorted input suggests two pointers or binary search. A contiguous subarray suggests a sliding window. A choice at each step where the locally best option is safe suggests greedy. Overlapping subproblems with an optimal substructure suggest dynamic programming. Enumerating all valid configurations suggests backtracking.
Naming the shape first prevents the most common failure mode: writing a correct-looking brute force, seeing it time out, and then patching it instead of replacing it.
bullets: Sorted or monotonic: two pointers, binary search
Contiguous window: sliding window
Count the ways or optimise over choices: dynamic programming
Locally best is provably safe: greedy
All valid arrangements: backtracking
Ordering with constraints: topological sort

sections.heading: Brute force first, then improve deliberately
body: Write the obviously correct version first, even if it is slow. It gives you test cases, and it makes the waste visible: which value is recomputed, which comparison is redundant, which scan could be a lookup.

Each optimisation should remove one specific waste. Replace a scan with a hash map, collapse a nested loop with a pointer, cache a repeated subproblem. Optimising without identifying the waste usually produces clever code with the same complexity.

keyPoints: Name the problem shape before writing code
Brute force first, then remove one waste at a time
State the complexity of your final solution out loud
Most optimisations replace a scan with a lookup or a nested loop with a pointer
Verify with a small hand-traced example before submitting

examples.title: Turning brute force into a sliding window
examples.body: A double loop checking every subarray becomes O(n) once you notice the inner bound only moves forward and the window's state can be updated incrementally.

examples.title: Turning recursion into DP
examples.body: A recursive solution that recomputes the same arguments gets a memo table keyed by those arguments. The shape of the code does not change; the repeated work disappears.

mistakes: Patching a brute force instead of changing the approach
Choosing DP where greedy is provably correct and simpler
Optimising before understanding the constraints
Not stating complexity, so nobody can check the reasoning
practiceTip: After each problem, write one sentence naming the technique. A list of those sentences is a personal pattern library.

subject: algo
name: Sorting
tagline: O(n log n) is the comparison barrier; know when to beat it
summary: Comparison-based sorting cannot beat O(n log n) in the worst case, which merge sort, heap sort and quicksort all reach. Counting and radix sort bypass the barrier when the keys are small integers.

sections.heading: The algorithms and their personalities
body: Merge sort splits, sorts each half and merges, guaranteeing O(n log n) with O(n) extra space and stable ordering. Heap sort builds a heap and extracts repeatedly, O(n log n) in place but not stable and with worse cache behaviour. Quicksort partitions around a pivot, O(n log n) average with O(n^2) worst case on adversarial input, but excellent constants and in-place operation.
Insertion sort is O(n^2) but unbeatable for tiny or nearly sorted inputs, which is why hybrid sorts use it below a size threshold.
bullets: Merge sort: stable, guaranteed O(n log n), needs O(n) space
Quicksort: fastest in practice, O(n^2) worst case without randomisation
Heap sort: in place, O(n log n), unstable
Counting/radix: O(n + k) when keys are bounded integers
Insertion sort: best for small or nearly sorted data

sections.heading: Beating the barrier with structure
body: Counting sort counts occurrences of each key in a bounded range and rebuilds the output, which is O(n + k) time and space. Radix sort applies a stable counting sort to each digit, giving O(d * (n + k)) for d digits.
Both require knowing something about the keys: a bounded range or fixed digit width. When that holds they beat every comparison sort, and the win is often the entire solution to the problem.

sections.heading: Sorting as a preprocessing step
body: Many problems stop being hard once the input is sorted: intervals merge in one pass, two-sum becomes two pointers, closest pair becomes a neighbour check, and duplicate detection becomes an adjacent comparison.
Remember the cost: if the problem needs only one pass after sorting, O(n log n) is the total, and that is often the intended complexity.

keyPoints: Comparison sorting has an O(n log n) lower bound
Merge sort is stable and guaranteed; quicksort is fastest on average
Heap sort is in place but unstable
Counting and radix sort beat the barrier on bounded integer keys
Sorting first turns many hard problems into a single pass

examples.title: Merging intervals
examples.body: Sort by start time, then walk once, merging whenever the next interval starts before the current one ends. Sorting makes the overlap check local, so one pass suffices.

examples.title: Sorting colours in one pass
examples.body: With only three values, counting sort uses O(1) space: count each value, then overwrite the array. No comparison sort needed.

mistakes: Using an unstable sort where stability matters
Quicksort with a fixed pivot on adversarial input
Sorting inside a loop, turning O(n log n) into O(n^2 log n)
Assuming the input is sorted when the contract does not say so
practiceTip: Implement merge sort and quicksort once each from scratch. The partition step in quicksort is worth knowing cold.

subject: algo
name: Binary Search
tagline: Halve the search space, but only when it is monotonic
summary: Binary search finds a target in a sorted array in O(log n) by halving the range each step. Its real power is that it works on any monotonic predicate, which lets you search over answers rather than over data.

sections.heading: The loop that everyone gets subtly wrong
body: Use left = 0, right = n - 1 and loop while left <= right. Compute mid with left + (right - left) / 2 to avoid overflow. If the middle value is too small, move left to mid + 1; if too large, move right to mid - 1.
The alternative boundary convention, half-open [left, right), uses while left < right and right = mid. Pick one and be consistent; mixing them is the classic off-by-one bug.
bullets: Always compute mid without overflow
Decide inclusive or half-open bounds and stick to it
Move by mid + 1 / mid - 1, never by 1, or you lose the logarithm
Binary search on the answer: find the smallest x where feasible(x) is true

sections.heading: Searching over the answer
body: The generalisation: if a predicate is monotonic, false for small inputs and true for large ones, binary search finds the boundary in O(log n) evaluations. Koko eating bananas, splitting an array into k subarrays, and minimum capacity to ship packages are all answer searches.
The work is proving monotonicity and writing the feasibility check. The search itself is three lines. This pattern solves a large fraction of hard interview problems.

sections.heading: Variants worth recognising
body: Lower bound finds the first index whose value is >= target; upper bound finds the first index whose value is > target. Finding the first or last occurrence of a duplicate is the same shape. Search in a rotated sorted array checks which half is properly ordered before deciding which side to discard.

keyPoints: Requires sorted data or a monotonic predicate
Halving each step gives O(log n)
Binary search on the answer works for any monotonic feasibility check
Compute mid without overflowing
Pick one boundary convention and never mix them

examples.title: First bad version
examples.body: Versions are monotonic: good before the first bad, bad after. Binary search for the first index where isBad is true, giving O(log n) calls.

examples.title: Koko eating bananas
examples.body: Feasibility, can she finish at speed k, is monotonic in k. Binary search the smallest feasible speed and check each candidate by summing ceil(pile / k).

mistakes: Using left < right with inclusive index arithmetic
Setting mid = (left + right) / 2 on large indices and overflowing
Assuming the array is sorted without checking
Discarding the wrong half when the predicate is not monotonic
practiceTip: Write lower_bound and upper_bound once each, then implement first-occurrence and last-occurrence as one-line callers.

subject: algo
name: Two Pointers & Sliding Window
tagline: Replace a nested loop with one forward-only pass
summary: Two pointers walk the input from both ends or at different speeds, and a sliding window keeps a contiguous range valid by advancing one end at a time. Both convert O(n^2) scans into O(n) by exploiting monotonicity or incremental state.

sections.heading: Opposite ends
body: With a sorted array, put one pointer at each end and move the one that improves the situation. Two-sum in a sorted array, container with most water, and reversing in place are all this pattern. The insight is that moving one pointer can be justified while moving both would not.
Without sortedness the pattern usually does not apply, and forcing it produces wrong answers.
bullets: Sorted pair problems: pointers from both ends
Palindrome checks: converge from both ends
Fast and slow pointers: cycle detection, middle of a list
Sliding window: contiguous subarray with a constraint

sections.heading: Sliding window, the incremental state trick
body: Expand the right pointer to add an element, then shrink from the left while the window is invalid, updating the answer whenever the window is valid. The cost is O(n) because each element enters and leaves the window once.
The state must be maintainable incrementally: a running sum, a frequency map, or a count of distinct elements. If updating the state costs more than O(1), the window is no longer linear.

keyPoints: Opposite-end pointers need sorted or symmetric structure
Fast and slow pointers detect cycles and find middles
A sliding window is valid only when the state updates in O(1)
Each element enters and leaves the window exactly once, giving O(n)
Both patterns remove the inner loop, not just speed it up

examples.title: Longest substring without repeats
examples.body: Track the last index of each character. When a repeat is inside the window, jump the left pointer past it. One pass with a map, O(n).

examples.title: Minimum window substring
examples.body: Expand until the window contains all required characters, then shrink from the left as far as possible while it still does, recording the shortest. Each index is visited twice at most.

mistakes: Applying opposite-end pointers to unsorted data
Letting the window state update cost more than O(1)
Shrinking only once instead of in a while loop
Forgetting to update the answer after shrinking
practiceTip: When a brute force has an inner loop that only moves forward, rewrite it as a window before reaching for anything fancier.

subject: algo
name: Dynamic Programming
tagline: Optimal substructure plus overlapping subproblems
summary: Dynamic programming solves a problem by expressing the answer in terms of smaller answers and caching those answers. It applies when subproblems repeat and the optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems.

sections.heading: The two conditions, checked honestly
body: Optimal substructure means the best solution to the whole is built from the best solutions to the parts. Overlapping subproblems means those parts recur, so recomputing them is waste. Both must hold; if subproblems never overlap, memoisation adds nothing and plain recursion is fine.
Counting problems also qualify: "how many ways" usually has optimal substructure in the sense that counts add up over the last choice, even though nothing is being optimised.
bullets: Define what a subproblem is, usually indexed by a suffix or prefix
Write the recurrence in words before code
Identify the base cases explicitly
Decide top-down memoisation or bottom-up table
State the dimensions and the resulting time and space

sections.heading: Top-down versus bottom-up
body: Top-down writes the recursion and adds a memo table, which is faster to get right and only computes needed states. Bottom-up fills a table in dependency order, which avoids recursion depth limits and often allows space optimisation.
If the recurrence only needs the previous row, a 2D table collapses to O(n) space. If it only needs a few previous values, keep those in variables. State the optimisation; interviewers expect it.

sections.heading: The classic families
body: Linear DP, one dimension: climbing stairs, house robber, maximum subarray. Knapsack family, a capacity dimension: subset sum, 0/1 knapsack, coin change. Interval DP, ranges of indices: matrix chain multiplication, palindrome partitioning. Grid DP, two dimensions: unique paths, edit distance. Tree DP: subtree aggregates.
The fastest way to get unstuck is to write the brute-force recursion, notice which arguments repeat, and add a memo table. That single move converts most exponential solutions into polynomial ones.

keyPoints: Requires optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems
Define the state, the recurrence and the base cases before coding
Top-down memoisation is easier; bottom-up avoids recursion limits
Collapse dimensions when the recurrence only needs the previous row
Brute-force recursion plus a memo table is the reliable path in

examples.title: Coin change
examples.body: State: fewest coins to make amount a. Recurrence: 1 + min over coins of dp[a - coin]. Bottom-up over amounts gives O(amount * coins) time and O(amount) space.

examples.title: Longest common subsequence
examples.body: Two-index state over both strings. If characters match, take the diagonal plus one; otherwise take the better of dropping one character from either string. O(m*n) time, collapsible to O(min(m, n)) space.

mistakes: Memoising without a base case, so nothing terminates
Defining the state too coarsely so subproblems still overlap
Filling a bottom-up table in the wrong order
Using DP where a greedy argument is correct and simpler
practiceTip: For every DP problem, write the state as a sentence beginning "dp[i] is the answer for..." before writing any code.

subject: algo
name: Greedy Algorithms
tagline: Take the locally best choice, and prove it is safe
summary: A greedy algorithm builds a solution by repeatedly taking the best-looking option. It is fast and simple, but only correct when the locally best choice can never block a better global solution, which must be argued, not assumed.

sections.heading: When greedy is provably correct
body: Greedy works when two properties hold: a greedy choice property, that some locally optimal choice is part of some global optimum, and optimal substructure. Interval scheduling, Huffman coding, Dijkstra's algorithm and Kruskal's MST all satisfy them.

The proof is usually an exchange argument: take any optimal solution and show it can be transformed into the greedy one without getting worse. If you cannot sketch that argument, greedy is probably wrong.
bullets: Sort by the right key first; the key is the whole algorithm
Interval scheduling: earliest finish time
Fractional knapsack: highest value per weight
Huffman coding: merge the two smallest frequencies
Activity and meeting-room problems: finish-time ordering

sections.heading: Greedy versus dynamic programming
body: If a local choice can invalidate a future better choice, greedy fails and DP is needed. The coin-change problem is the standard illustration: with coins 1, 3, 4 and target 6, greedy takes 4 then 1 then 1 for three coins, while 3 + 3 uses two.
The tell is a counterexample. Spending thirty seconds looking for one is the cheapest way to decide between greedy and DP.

keyPoints: Correct only with a greedy choice property plus optimal substructure
Prove it with an exchange argument, or look for a counterexample
The sort key usually carries the entire algorithm
Greedy is O(n log n) or better when DP would be polynomial
Counterexamples are the fastest way to reject greedy

examples.title: Maximum non-overlapping meetings
examples.body: Sort by finish time and take every meeting that starts after the last chosen one ends. The exchange argument shows any solution can be rewritten this way without losing meetings.

examples.title: Jump game reachability
examples.body: Track the furthest index reachable and update it as you walk. If the current index passes the furthest reach, the end is unreachable. One pass, O(n).

mistakes: Assuming greedy works without a proof or counterexample check
Sorting by the wrong key, such as start time instead of finish time
Applying greedy to 0/1 knapsack, where only the fractional version works
Missing a tie-breaking rule that changes the outcome
practiceTip: Before coding a greedy solution, write one sentence explaining why the local choice cannot hurt. If you cannot, write the DP instead.

subject: algo
name: Recursion & Backtracking
tagline: Enumerate choices, undo them, and let the stack hold the path
summary: Recursion solves a problem by solving smaller instances of itself. Backtracking extends this to enumeration: try each choice, recurse, and undo the choice before trying the next, which explores the whole search space while keeping memory proportional to depth.

sections.heading: Every recursive function has the same three parts
body: A base case that stops the recursion, a step that reduces the problem toward the base case, and a call that trusts the recursion for the reduced problem. If any part is missing, the function either never returns or never terminates.

The order of work relative to the recursive call gives the three orders: before the call is pre-order, after is post-order, and between two calls on subranges is in-order. Tree traversals are exactly this.
bullets: Always write the base case first
Make progress toward it on every branch
Trust the recursion; do not trace it in your head
Watch the depth: deep recursion needs an explicit stack

sections.heading: Backtracking is recursion with an undo step
body: Choose an option, recurse, then un-choose it so the next option starts from the same state. Permutations, combinations, subsets, N-queens and word search are all this shape. The visited set or the mutation plus restore is what makes the enumeration correct.
Pruning is where the speed comes from: cut branches that cannot lead to a valid answer before recursing. A well-pruned backtracking solution can beat a clever DP, and it is usually easier to write.

sections.heading: Subsets, permutations, combinations
body: For subsets, at each element decide include or exclude, producing 2^n results. For permutations, fix each unused element at the current position and recurse, producing n! results. For combinations of size k, add elements in increasing order to avoid duplicates.
Because the output itself is exponential, no algorithm can do better; the goal is O(output size), which these templates achieve.

keyPoints: Base case, reduction step, recursive call, in that order
Work before the call is pre-order, after is post-order
Backtracking is choose, recurse, un-choose
Prune branches early; that is where the performance lives
Exponential output means O(output) is optimal

examples.title: N-queens
examples.body: Place a queen per row, tracking occupied columns and diagonals in sets. Recurse to the next row, and undo the placement when returning. Pruning by the diagonal sets removes almost all of the search space.

examples.title: Word search in a grid
examples.body: From each cell, DFS matching the next character, marking the cell visited and unmarking on return. The mark is the undo step; without it the search wanders in circles.

mistakes: Missing or unreachable base cases
Forgetting to un-choose, so later branches see stale state
Not pruning, turning a tractable search into an explosion
Recursing deeper than the stack allows on large inputs
practiceTip: Write the backtracking template once, with choose, recurse and un-choose clearly separated. Every enumeration problem then becomes filling in three lines.

subject: algo
name: Graph Algorithms
tagline: Traversal plus the right bookkeeping
summary: Graph algorithms are traversals with extra state: distances, discovery times, indegrees or component labels. Knowing which state to track is what separates Dijkstra from BFS from topological sort.

sections.heading: Shortest paths, by weight type
body: Unweighted: BFS with a queue gives shortest paths in O(V + E). Non-negative weights: Dijkstra with a min-heap, O((V + E) log V). Negative weights: Bellman-Ford, O(V * E), which also detects negative cycles. All pairs on a small graph: Floyd-Warshall, O(V^3).
Choosing BFS where Dijkstra is needed is the classic mistake: BFS ignores edge weights entirely and returns hop counts, not distances.
bullets: Unweighted shortest path: BFS
Non-negative weighted: Dijkstra with a heap
Negative weights: Bellman-Ford
All pairs, small V: Floyd-Warshall
Dependencies and ordering: topological sort

sections.heading: Minimum spanning tree and components
body: Kruskal sorts all edges and adds each one that joins two different components, using union-find, for O(E log E). Prim grows one tree by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge to an outside vertex, using a heap, for O(E log V). Both produce the same total weight.
For components, union-find or a simple DFS labelling is enough; the difference is whether edges arrive incrementally, which union-find handles and a fresh DFS does not.

sections.heading: Topological order and cycle detection
body: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes vertices with indegree zero, which produces a valid order and detects a cycle when vertices remain. A DFS variant pushes a vertex after all its descendants, then reverses the result.
Strongly connected components, via Kosaraju or Tarjan, generalise this to directed graphs where cycles are unavoidable; each SCC is a single vertex in the condensation.

keyPoints: BFS for unweighted, Dijkstra for non-negative weights, Bellman-Ford for negatives
Kruskal uses union-find; Prim uses a heap; both give the MST weight
Topological sort exists only on a DAG
Kahn's indegree method both orders and detects cycles
Tarjan or Kosaraju finds strongly connected components

examples.title: Network delay time
examples.body: Dijkstra from the source over all nodes; the answer is the largest final distance. BFS would be wrong because the edges have different weights.

examples.title: Course schedule feasibility
examples.body: Build the directed graph and run Kahn's algorithm. If the produced order contains every course, the schedule is possible; a leftover vertex means a cycle.

mistakes: Using BFS on weighted edges
Running Dijkstra with negative weights
Marking visited on finish instead of discovery
Assuming an undirected graph when the input is directed
practiceTip: Keep one generic BFS/DFS helper and adapt it. The differences between Dijkstra, topological sort and component labelling are only the bookkeeping.

subject: aptitude
name: Quantitative Aptitude
tagline: Percentages, ratios and time-speed, fast and exactly
summary: Aptitude questions are arithmetic with a time limit. The skill is not long division but recognising the structure: percentages, ratios and inverse proportionality convert most questions into one or two short steps.

sections.heading: Percentages are fractions in disguise
body: A percentage change followed by the reverse change is not a return to the start: a 20% rise then a 20% fall leaves 96 percent of the original, because the two percentages apply to different bases. Working in multipliers makes this automatic.
Successive changes multiply. Three changes of +10%, +20% and -10% are 1.1 times 1.2 times 0.9, which is 1.188, an 18.8 percent net rise.
bullets: x% of y equals y% of x; pick the easier order
Successive percentage changes multiply
Fraction equivalents: 12.5% is 1/8, 37.5% is 3/8
Profit and loss are percentages on cost price unless stated
Simple interest is linear; compound interest multiplies

sections.heading: Ratios and inverse relations
body: A ratio a:b means the parts share a total in those proportions, so scaling the ratio scales the share. Time, speed and distance are inversely related at fixed distance, and time and work are inversely related at fixed rate.
For work problems, convert every person into a rate. If A finishes in 6 days and B in 12, their rates are 1/6 and 1/12 per day, and together they finish in 1/(1/6 + 1/12) days.

keyPoints: A percentage rise and an equal fall do not cancel
Successive changes multiply, they do not add
Ratios scale shares; inverse relations underpin time-speed and work
Convert people and machines to rates before combining
Memorise common fraction equivalents to save time

examples.title: Successive discounts
examples.body: Two successive 10 percent discounts give 0.9 times 0.9, or 0.81, which is a single 19 percent discount, not 20 percent.

examples.title: Pipes filling a tank
examples.body: One pipe fills in 20 minutes and another in 30. Rates are 1/20 and 1/30 per minute, together 1/12, so the tank fills in 12 minutes.

mistakes: Adding percentages that apply to different bases
Using cost price where selling price was meant
Adding rates instead of adding their reciprocals
Forgetting unit conversions in speed problems
practiceTip: Convert every percentage to a fraction the moment you read it. The arithmetic that follows is usually two lines.

subject: reasoning
name: Logical Reasoning
tagline: Follow the rule, not the plausibility
summary: Logical reasoning questions supply a rule and ask what follows. The discipline is to answer from the rule alone, and to resist options that are merely true in the everyday world.

sections.heading: Syllogisms: what follows, not what is likely
body: With 'all A are B' and 'some B are C', it does not follow that any A is a C. The C that are B need not be the B that are A. Drawing Venn diagrams removes the guesswork.
The reliable move is to test each conclusion by trying to construct a case where the premises hold and the conclusion fails. If you can, the conclusion does not follow.
bullets: All A are B does not imply all B are A
Some A are B does not imply some B are not A
A conclusion follows only if no counterexample is possible
Draw the diagram rather than reasoning by feel

sections.heading: Series, coding and arrangement
body: Number series usually hide arithmetic progressions in the differences, or two interleaved series. Letter series often work on positions with shifting gaps. Coding questions map symbols consistently, so write the mapping down before answering.
Seating and arrangement problems are constraint satisfaction. Start from the fixed points, the clues that name an absolute position, and only then place the relative clues.

keyPoints: Answer from the stated rule, not from everyday plausibility
A conclusion follows only if no counterexample exists
Check second differences when a series is not arithmetic
Write the code mapping before answering
Place absolute clues first in arrangement problems

examples.title: The trap in syllogisms
examples.body: All roses are flowers and some flowers fade quickly does not imply some roses fade quickly, because the fading flowers need not be roses.

examples.title: Two interleaved series
examples.body: A series that alternates between one arithmetic progression and another looks irregular until you split it into odd and even positions.

mistakes: Choosing the answer that sounds true rather than the one that follows
Assuming a series is arithmetic before checking second differences
Guessing in arrangement problems instead of fixing absolute positions
Inventing a mapping beyond the one given
practiceTip: For each reasoning question, state the rule in your own words first. Misreading the rule is the most common cause of a wrong answer.

subject: accounting
name: Accounting Basics
tagline: Every transaction twice, and it must still balance
summary: Accounting records every transaction in at least two accounts so that the books stay balanced. The three statements then describe the same business from three angles: position, performance, and cash.

sections.heading: Double entry and the accounting equation
body: Assets equal liabilities plus equity. Every transaction changes at least two accounts so the equation stays true, which is the check that makes the whole system self-verifying.
Debits increase assets and expenses; credits increase liabilities, equity and revenue. The words are conventional, not directional: a debit is simply the left side of an account.
bullets: Assets = liabilities + equity, always
Debits increase assets and expenses
Credits increase liabilities, equity and revenue
Accrual basis records when earned, not when paid
The trial balance proves the ledger balances

sections.heading: The three statements
body: The balance sheet shows position at a point in time. The income statement shows performance over a period, revenue minus expenses. The cash flow statement shows actual cash movement, split into operating, investing and financing.
Profit and cash differ mainly through accruals and non-cash items such as depreciation, which is why a profitable company can still run out of cash.

keyPoints: Assets equal liabilities plus equity at all times
Every transaction has at least two entries
Debits increase assets and expenses; credits the rest
Depreciation is non-cash, so profit and cash diverge
The three statements describe position, performance and cash

examples.title: Buying equipment on credit
examples.body: Assets rise by the equipment value and liabilities rise by the same amount, so the equation holds. No cash moves, which is why the cash flow statement is unaffected at that moment.

examples.title: Profitable but out of cash
examples.body: Sales are recorded on credit, increasing profit and receivables, while cash leaves for expenses. Profit is high but cash is low until receivables are collected.

mistakes: Treating a debit as a decrease
Confusing profit with cash
Ignoring depreciation as a real cost
Recording a transaction in only one account
practiceTip: For any transaction, state the two accounts affected before writing the entry. If you cannot find two, you have missed part of the transaction.

subject: dbms
name: Databases & SQL
tagline: Modelled data, queried declaratively, kept consistent
summary: A relational database stores data in relations with declared constraints, and queries it declaratively: you say what you want, and the optimizer decides how to get it. Most database skill is modelling well and then reading what the plan is doing.

sections.heading: Declarative means the plan matters
body: SQL describes the result, not the procedure. Two identical-looking queries can differ by orders of magnitude depending on whether the optimizer used an index, which is why reading EXPLAIN output is a core skill rather than an advanced one.
A missing index on a join or filter column turns a scan into a full table scan. An unselective index can be worse than none. Cost estimates, not rules of thumb, decide.
bullets: Model first: entities, keys, constraints
Normalize to remove redundancy, denormalize for measured read cost
Filter and join columns are the index candidates
Read EXPLAIN before optimising anything
Transactions carry the consistency guarantees

sections.heading: SQL is set-based
body: Thinking in sets instead of loops is the main translation. Aggregation with GROUP BY and HAVING, window functions for running and ranked values, and set operators for combining results cover most needs. Row-by-row processing in application code usually duplicates what one query could do.
The common performance mistake is the N+1 pattern: one query for a list, then one per row for details. A join or a single IN query replaces the loop.

keyPoints: SQL is declarative; the plan decides the cost
Read EXPLAIN before optimising
Index the filter and join columns
Think in sets, not row loops
Constraints are cheaper than application-side validation

examples.title: The N+1 pattern
examples.body: Loading a page of orders and then querying the customer for each one costs one query plus N queries. A single join, or one query with IN, reduces it to one round trip.

examples.title: Ranked results without a self-join
examples.body: A window function such as ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) produces ranks in one pass, replacing a correlated subquery per row.

mistakes: Optimising before reading the plan
Selecting star instead of the needed columns on wide tables
Storing comma-separated values in a single column
Assuming a query is fast because the table is small today
practiceTip: For every query you write, ask what index the optimizer would choose and why. If you cannot say, run EXPLAIN.

subject: dbms
name: Normalization
tagline: Remove redundancy by moving dependencies into their own tables
summary: Normalization reorganises tables so that each fact is stored once, which prevents update, insert and delete anomalies. The normal forms are a sequence of requirements about what a table's primary key determines.

sections.heading: The forms as a sequence
body: First normal form requires atomic values and no repeating groups. Second requires every non-key column to depend on the whole key, not part of it. Third goes further: no non-key column may depend on another non-key column, which means no transitive dependencies.
BCNF tightens the third form's dependency rule. In practice, reaching BCNF on every table is rarely worth the join count, and many production schemas stop at third normal form deliberately.
bullets: 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
2NF: no partial dependency on part of a composite key
3NF: no transitive dependency between non-key columns
BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key
Denormalize only for a measured read cost

sections.heading: The anomalies you are removing
body: Update anomaly: one fact stored in many rows, so changing it means many changes and inconsistency is possible. Insert anomaly: unrelated data cannot be recorded because something else is missing. Delete anomaly: removing one fact destroys another that had no other home.
Naming the anomaly a normalization prevents is the standard way to answer why it matters, and it is a more convincing answer than citing the form number.

keyPoints: 1NF atomic, 2NF no partial dependency, 3NF no transitive dependency
Normalization removes update, insert and delete anomalies
A functional dependency is what the forms are actually about
BCNF is stricter than 3NF and often unnecessary in practice
Denormalization is a performance decision, not a modelling one

examples.title: Splitting a course table
examples.body: A row holding course, instructor and instructor office stores the office once per student enrolled, so changing the office means many updates. Moving instructor details to their own table with a foreign key removes that anomaly.

examples.title: Transitive dependency
examples.body: Order rows storing zip code and city mean the city is determined by the zip, which is determined by the order key. City depends transitively, so it belongs in a zip-code table.

mistakes: Normalizing to BCNF everywhere without measuring the join cost
Storing multiple values in one column to dodge 1NF
Ignoring the anomalies and only citing form numbers
Treating denormalization as inherently bad
practiceTip: For each table you design, name the anomalies its structure prevents. That sentence is usually the whole normalization answer.

subject: dbms
name: Transactions & Concurrency
tagline: ACID is a contract, and isolation levels are a dial
summary: A transaction is a unit of work that is atomic, consistent, isolated and durable. Isolation is not binary: levels from read committed to serializable trade correctness guarantees against concurrency and throughput.

sections.heading: ACID, one promise at a time
body: Atomicity means all or nothing, implemented with an undo log. Consistency means constraints hold before and after, which is the application's definition as much as the database's. Isolation means concurrent transactions do not see each other's intermediate states. Durability means committed data survives a crash, typically via a write-ahead log flushed before the commit returns.
Knowing which mechanism implements which property is what turns the acronym into an answer.
bullets: Atomicity: undo log
Durability: write-ahead log, flushed on commit
Isolation: locking or MVCC snapshots
Consistency: declared constraints plus application rules

sections.heading: Isolation levels and the anomalies they allow
body: Read committed prevents dirty reads. Repeatable read also prevents non-repeatable reads. Serializable additionally prevents phantom reads, and is the only level that behaves like sequential execution. Snapshot isolation in MVCC databases gives repeatable reads cheaply but allows write skew.
Read uncommitted allows dirty reads and is almost never appropriate. Choosing a level is a deliberate decision about which anomalies your application can tolerate.
bullets: Dirty read: reading another transaction's uncommitted write
Non-repeatable read: a row changes between two reads
Phantom read: a range gains or loses rows between reads
Write skew: two transactions read overlapping data and both write

sections.heading: Locking and MVCC
body: Two-phase locking acquires locks and releases them only at the end, which gives serializability but risks deadlock and reduces concurrency. MVCC keeps multiple versions of a row so readers never block writers, at the cost of version cleanup and some anomalies.
Deadlocks are detected or avoided by lock ordering, exactly as in the OS case, and the usual resolution is to abort one transaction and retry.

keyPoints: Atomicity via undo, durability via write-ahead logging
Read committed is the common default
Serializable is the only level equal to sequential execution
Dirty, non-repeatable, phantom and write skew are distinct anomalies
Two-phase locking gives serializability; MVCC gives cheap reads

examples.title: Transfer between accounts
examples.body: Debit and credit must both happen or neither, so they share a transaction. With serializable isolation, two concurrent transfers cannot interleave into a lost update.

examples.title: Report versus checkout
examples.body: A nightly report tolerates stale reads and can use snapshot isolation. A balance check that gates a payment needs repeatable read or serializable to avoid deciding on a value that changes underneath it.

mistakes: Assuming read committed prevents phantoms
Using higher isolation without measuring the contention cost
Retrying a deadlocked transaction without changing the lock order
Treating durability as guaranteed without a flush on commit
practiceTip: For each isolation level, write the anomaly it still permits. The table of level-to-anomaly is the entire answer.

mistakes: Left join then COUNT(*) inflating results
Filtering on an aggregate in WHERE instead of HAVING
Using DISTINCT to hide a join duplication bug
Joining on columns without indexes
subject: dbms

bullets: Inner: only matching rows
Left: all left rows, nulls on the right
Semi-join: filter by existence, do not duplicate
Anti-join: filter by non-existence
body: An inner join keeps only rows matching on both sides. A left join keeps every left row and nulls the right side where nothing matches, which is why counting after a left join can double-count.
Choosing between them is a question about which side is authoritative. If every order must appear even without a customer, a left join is required.
sections.heading: Joins decide the row count

bullets: WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups
Window functions keep rows and add computed columns
PARTITION BY sets the window, ORDER BY sets the order within it
Running totals are SUM() OVER (ORDER BY ...)
body: GROUP BY collapses rows into groups, and HAVING filters after the collapse while WHERE filters before. Window functions compute across a partition while keeping every row, which is how running totals and ranks are expressed in one pass.
Reaching for a correlated subquery where a window function would do is the usual performance loss.
sections.heading: Aggregation and window functions

practiceTip: Write every query twice: once with subqueries and once with joins or window functions. Compare the plans.
name: SQL Queries
summary: SQL expresses what to retrieve over sets of rows. Joins combine relations, GROUP BY aggregates them, and window functions compute values across a partition without collapsing rows.

examples.body: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at) gives a running total per customer in one pass, without a self-join.
examples.title: Running total per customer

examples.body: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group_id ORDER BY score DESC) then filtering on row number one gives the best row per group, replacing a correlated subquery.
examples.title: Top row per group

keyPoints: Inner join matches, left join preserves the left side
WHERE filters before grouping, HAVING after
Window functions compute without collapsing rows
Correlated subqueries are usually replaceable by a join
Count distinct to avoid double counting after a join
tagline: Joins, aggregation and window functions

mistakes: Indexing every column on a write-heavy table
Wrong column order in a composite index
Expecting a hash index to serve a range query
Ignoring the plan and adding indexes on suspicion
subject: dbms

bullets: B-tree: equality and range
Hash: equality only
Composite: leftmost prefix rule applies
Covering: answers the query without a table lookup
Unique: also enforces a constraint
body: A B-tree index stores keys in sorted order with pointers to rows, so equality and range lookups are both logarithmic. A hash index maps a key to a bucket, giving O(1) equality but no ordering, so it cannot serve range queries.
A covering index includes every column the query needs, so the engine can answer from the index alone without touching the table. That is often the largest single win available.
sections.heading: What an index actually is

body: Every insert, update and delete must maintain each index, so write-heavy tables pay per index. An unselective index on a column with few distinct values is often ignored by the optimizer because a scan is cheaper.
The decision is data-driven: look at the query workload and the plan, then add the index that removes a scan. Indexing every column is a common well-meant mistake that slows everything down.
sections.heading: Cost and when not to

practiceTip: Before adding an index, run EXPLAIN and identify the exact scan you are removing.
name: Indexing
summary: An index is a separate structure that lets the engine find rows without scanning the table. A B-tree index serves range and equality queries, a hash index serves equality only, and each index slows writes and consumes space.

examples.body: An index on (last_name, first_name) serves queries filtering on last_name alone, but not queries filtering on first_name alone, because the prefix rule requires the leftmost column.
examples.title: Composite index order

examples.body: A dashboard query selecting id, status and created_at can be answered entirely from an index on those columns, removing every table access from the plan.
examples.title: Covering index win

keyPoints: B-tree serves equality and range; hash serves equality only
A composite index is used leftmost-first
A covering index avoids the table lookup entirely
Each index costs write throughput and space
Unselective indexes are usually ignored
tagline: Trade write cost and space for read speed

subject: ds
name: Data Structures
tagline: How data is organised decides what your code can do fast
summary: A data structure is a way of organising data so that the operations you actually perform become cheap. Choosing one is an engineering trade between access time, memory, and how much code you are willing to maintain.

sections.heading: Pick the structure from the operation, not the name
body: The wrong question is "which structure is best". The right question is "which operation happens most often, and what does it currently cost". A list is fine for appending, terrible for random access; a hash map is excellent for lookup, useless for ordered traversal.
Write the hot path down first: search, insert, delete, range query, min/max, or ordered iteration. Every structure below is a bet on one of those.
bullets: Random access by index: array
Frequent insert/delete at the ends: deque, linked list
Exact lookup: hash table
Ordered traversal or range queries: balanced tree, sorted array
Always-need-the-smallest: heap

sections.heading: Trade-offs are the whole subject
body: Nothing is free. A hash table buys O(1) lookup with unordered iteration and memory overhead. A balanced tree buys ordering with a constant factor larger than hashing. An array buys locality and cache speed with expensive middle insertion.
Say the cost out loud when you choose: "search will be O(log n) and iteration stays sorted, at the cost of a heavier insert". That sentence is what an interviewer is listening for.

keyPoints: Choose from the operation you perform most, not from the structure's name
Every choice trades time, memory and code complexity
State the complexity and the trade-off explicitly when you decide
Cache locality matters as much as asymptotics for small inputs
Revisit the choice when the access pattern changes

examples.title: Counting word frequencies
examples.body: An array of strings forces an O(n) scan per word. A hash map keyed by word makes it O(1) per word and the code gets shorter, not longer.

examples.title: Keeping the top 10 scores
examples.body: Sorting after every score is O(n log n) each time. A fixed-size min-heap keeps it O(log 10) per score, and the code expresses the intent directly.

mistakes: Reaching for the most complex structure before measuring
Ignoring the constant factor for small inputs
Choosing ordered iteration when the code never iterates in order
Assuming hash tables keep insertion order
practiceTip: For each structure below, write the one-line rule for when you would reach for it. Then check your last three pieces of code against that rule.

subject: ds
name: Arrays
tagline: Contiguous memory, O(1) indexing, expensive middles
summary: An array stores elements in one contiguous block, so the address of element i is base + i * size. That single fact gives O(1) indexing and excellent cache behaviour, and makes insertion or deletion in the middle O(n) because everything after it must shift.

sections.heading: Why indexing is O(1) and insertion is not
body: Contiguity is the whole story. Knowing the start address and the element size is enough to compute any element's address directly, which is why a[i] costs the same time whether the array holds 10 elements or 10 million.

Inserting in the middle breaks that: every later element must move one slot right, so the cost grows with the number of elements after the insertion point. Appending at the end is amortised O(1) when capacity is doubled, because the expensive reallocation happens rarely and is spread across many cheap appends.

sections.heading: The patterns that matter
body: Most array problems reduce to a handful of patterns: prefix sums for range queries, two pointers for sorted or paired data, sliding windows for contiguous subarrays, and in-place swaps or reversals when extra memory is forbidden.
When you are asked to avoid extra space, remember that you can often overwrite the input: mark visited entries, use the sign bit, or reverse in place with two indices.
bullets: Prefix sums turn repeated range sums into O(1) lookups
Two pointers replace a nested loop when the array is sorted
Sliding window handles contiguous windows in O(n)
Sorting first often turns a quadratic problem into a linear one

sections.heading: Complexity summary
body: Access by index O(1), search in an unsorted array O(n), search in a sorted array O(log n) with binary search, insert at the end amortised O(1), insert or delete in the middle O(n).

Space is O(n) with a small constant, and the elements sit next to each other in memory, which is why iterating an array is dramatically faster than iterating a linked list despite identical asymptotic complexity.

keyPoints: Indexing is O(1) because the address is computed arithmetically
Middle insert/delete is O(n) because elements shift
Appending is amortised O(1) when capacity doubles
Cache locality makes arrays the fastest structure to scan
Prefix sums, two pointers and sliding windows solve most array problems

examples.title: Two-sum in a sorted array
examples.body: Put one pointer at each end and move inward based on the sum. Sorted input plus two pointers turns the O(n^2) double loop into a single O(n) pass with O(1) extra space.

examples.title: Range sum asked many times
examples.body: Precompute prefix sums once in O(n); each query then costs O(1). The trade is O(n) extra memory for the prefix array.

mistakes: Off-by-one in loops, especially with inclusive ranges
Forgetting that shifting makes middle insertion O(n)
Not handling empty or single-element input
Mutating the input when the caller still needs it
practiceTip: Implement binary search from scratch until you can write both the leftmost and rightmost variants without looking anything up.

subject: ds
name: Linked Lists
tagline: Cheap splicing, no random access
summary: A linked list stores each element in its own node with a pointer to the next. Inserting or removing a node is O(1) once you hold the node before it, but reaching index i costs O(i) because you must walk the chain. It is the mirror image of an array's trade-offs.

sections.heading: The operations, honestly costed
body: Access by index O(n), search O(n), insert at the head O(1), insert after a known node O(1), delete a known node O(1). Nothing is O(1) by index, and no operation is free of the pointer chase.
Because nodes are allocated separately, iteration touches scattered memory and performs far worse in practice than an array scan of the same length, even though both are O(n).
bullets: Singly linked: forward only, minimal memory
Doubly linked: backward traversal and O(1) delete given the node
Circular: no null check at the end, useful for round-robin
Sentinel/dummy head: removes most special cases

sections.heading: The four patterns worth knowing
body: Reverse the list by walking once and flipping next pointers, keeping three variables: previous, current, next. Detect a cycle with Floyd's tortoise and hare, two pointers at different speeds. Find the middle by advancing a fast pointer two steps for every one of a slow pointer. Merge two sorted lists by repeatedly taking the smaller head.
Every linked-list interview question is one of those four, plus the discipline of drawing the pointer before you touch it. A drawing prevents the single most common bug: losing the rest of the list.

keyPoints: No random access; walking to index i is O(i)
Insert/delete is O(1) given the previous node
Memory is one node per element plus pointer overhead
Reverse, cycle detection, middle finding and merging are the core patterns
Draw the pointers before changing them

examples.title: Reversing in place
examples.body: Keep prev, curr and next. Point curr at prev, then slide all three forward. Ends with the old tail as the new head, using O(1) extra space.

examples.title: Removing the nth node from the end
examples.body: Advance a fast pointer n steps, then move fast and slow together until fast reaches the end. Slow then sits on the node before the target, so the deletion is O(1) after one O(n) pass.

mistakes: Losing the remainder of the list by overwriting next too early
Forgetting to update the tail when appending
Not freeing removed nodes in languages without GC
Using a linked list when random access dominates
practiceTip: Write a doubly linked list with a sentinel head and tail once. After that, no list problem needs special cases.

subject: ds
name: Stacks
tagline: Last in, first out — the structure of nesting
summary: A stack supports push, pop and peek, all O(1), and only at one end. Its power is that it reverses order and remembers the most recent unresolved thing, which is exactly what nesting, undo and expression parsing need.

sections.heading: Where stacks come from
body: The call stack is a stack: each call pushes a frame, each return pops one. Undo histories, browser back buttons, bracket matching, depth-first traversal and expression evaluation are all the same shape.
The signal that a stack is the answer is the phrase "most recent unresolved item". If your algorithm needs to remember what you were in the middle of, a stack remembers it for you.
bullets: Balanced parentheses: push opens, pop on closes, compare
Monotonic stack: keeps candidates for the next greater/smaller element
Next greater element: pop while the top is smaller, that is the answer
DFS iteratively: push neighbours instead of recursing

sections.heading: The monotonic stack pattern
body: A monotonic stack keeps its elements in sorted order by discarding entries that can never be an answer again. For "next greater element", every value smaller than the current one is popped because the current element is a better answer for everything they might have served.
Each element is pushed and popped at most once, so the whole scan is O(n) despite the nested-looking while loop.

keyPoints: Push, pop and peek are all O(1)
It reverses order and remembers the most recent item
Balanced brackets and DFS are the canonical uses
A monotonic stack solves next-greater/next-smaller in O(n)
Deep recursion can be converted to an explicit stack

examples.title: Balanced brackets
examples.body: Scan once, pushing openers and popping on closers. If a pop mismatches or the stack is non-empty at the end, the string is unbalanced. One pass, O(n) time and space.

examples.title: Daily temperatures
examples.body: Keep a stack of indices whose warmer day is still unknown. When a warmer day arrives, pop and record the difference. Each index enters and leaves once.

mistakes: Popping from an empty stack
Forgetting the final empty-stack check in bracket problems
Recursing where an explicit stack avoids stack overflow
Confusing LIFO order with queue order
practiceTip: Implement an iterative DFS with an explicit stack, then compare it with the recursive version to see which parts of the recursion the stack is doing for you.

subject: ds
name: Queues & Deques
tagline: First in, first out — the structure of waiting
summary: A queue adds at the back and removes from the front, both O(1). It models anything that must be handled in arrival order: work queues, breadth-first search, and rate limiting. A deque extends this by allowing both operations at both ends.

sections.heading: Queues are level order
body: Breadth-first search is a queue: put the start node in, then repeatedly take the front, process it, and push its unseen neighbours. Because the queue preserves arrival order, nodes are visited in non-decreasing distance from the start, which is why BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
Using recursion or a stack instead gives depth-first order, which explores one branch fully before the next and does not guarantee shortest paths.
bullets: BFS shortest path in unweighted graphs: queue
Level-order traversal of a tree: queue
Sliding window maximum: monotonic deque
Task scheduling with fairness: queue

sections.heading: The monotonic deque
body: For a sliding window maximum, keep a deque of candidate indices whose values decrease from front to back. When a new value arrives, drop every smaller value from the back, since they can never be the maximum while the new one is in the window. The front is always the current maximum.
Each index is added and removed at most once, so the whole scan is O(n) rather than O(n*k) for a naive window scan.

keyPoints: Enqueue and dequeue are O(1) at opposite ends
BFS and level-order traversal are queue patterns
A deque supports both ends, which unlocks sliding-window problems
A monotonic deque gives window maxima in O(n)
Queues give breadth-first order; stacks give depth-first

examples.title: Shortest path in a grid
examples.body: Start from the source cell in a queue, expand neighbours in four directions, and record the distance when each cell is first seen. First arrival is the shortest distance because BFS explores in layers.

examples.title: Sliding window maximum
examples.body: Maintain a monotonic deque of indices. Push each index after removing smaller values from the back, drop the front when it leaves the window, and read the maximum from the front.

mistakes: Marking nodes visited on push instead of on pop, which can enqueue duplicates
Using a stack and expecting BFS order
Forgetting to remove indices that slid out of the window
Confusing priority queues (heaps) with plain queues
practiceTip: Write BFS so that the first time you see a node you both enqueue and mark it. That single discipline removes the duplicate-enqueue bug.

subject: ds
name: Hashing & Hash Maps
tagline: O(1) average lookup, at the cost of ordering
summary: A hash map stores key-value pairs in buckets chosen by a hash of the key. Lookup, insert and delete are O(1) on average, but iteration order is not the insertion order and worst case is O(n) if hashes collide badly.

sections.heading: How a hash map actually works
body: The key is hashed to an integer, reduced modulo the bucket count to pick a bucket, and stored there. Collisions are handled either by chaining, a small list per bucket, or by open addressing, which probes for the next free slot.

When the load factor, entries divided by buckets, grows past a threshold, the table is rehashed into a larger array. That rehash is why individual inserts can occasionally be slow while the amortised cost stays O(1).

sections.heading: The patterns that make interviews easy
body: Hashing converts "have I seen this before" into a single lookup. Complements are the other half: for a target sum, store what you have seen and check whether target minus current is already present. Frequency counting replaces repeated scanning. Grouping by a canonical key, such as a sorted string, clusters anagrams.
The cost is that keys must be hashable and comparable for equality, and you give up ordering. If you need sorted iteration, a tree is the answer instead.
bullets: Seen-set: dedupe and cycle detection
Complement lookup: two-sum style problems in one pass
Frequency map: counting, majority element, first unique
Canonical key: anagram grouping, board state memoisation
Prefix sums in a map: subarray sums equal to k

keyPoints: Average O(1) lookup, insert and delete; worst case O(n)
A bad hash function or heavy collisions degrade everything
Iteration order is not guaranteed to be insertion order
Seen-sets and complement lookups replace nested loops
Rehashing makes a single insert occasionally expensive

examples.title: Two-sum in one pass
examples.body: Walk the array once, and before inserting each value check whether target minus value is already in the map. O(n) time instead of O(n^2), using O(n) space for the map.

examples.title: Grouping anagrams
examples.body: Use the sorted characters of each word as the map key. Words with the same sorted key are anagrams, so grouping costs one pass plus a sort per word.

mistakes: Using a mutable object as a key whose hash can change
Assuming insertion or sorted order
Ignoring the O(n) worst case in adversarial inputs
Using a hash map where a sorted structure was required
practiceTip: Before writing any nested loop, ask whether a hash map keyed on the inner value would collapse it into one pass.

subject: ds
name: Binary Trees & BSTs
tagline: Hierarchy, with ordered search on the side
summary: A binary tree gives each node at most two children. When the left subtree holds smaller values and the right holds larger ones it becomes a binary search tree, and search, insert and delete drop to O(log n) provided the tree stays balanced.

sections.heading: The traversals and when each fits
body: In-order traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order, which is why an in-order walk is the standard way to validate or to flatten a BST. Pre-order visits the node before its children, which is the natural serialisation order. Post-order visits children first, which is what you need when a node's value depends on its subtree, such as computing heights or freeing memory.
Level-order traversal uses a queue and visits the tree layer by layer. Every tree problem is one of these four orders plus a small amount of per-node work.
bullets: In-order: sorted output, BST validation
Pre-order: copying, serialising, prefix expressions
Post-order: heights, subtree sums, deletion
Level-order: depth, width, right-side view

sections.heading: BST operations and the balance catch
body: Search compares against the current node and goes left or right, halving the search space each step: O(log n) when balanced, O(n) in the degenerate case. Insertion follows the same path to a leaf. Deletion has three cases: no child, one child, and two children, where the node is replaced by its in-order successor or predecessor.

The catch is that inserting sorted data into a plain BST produces a linked list. Self-balancing trees, AVL and red-black, fix this by rotating during insert and delete to keep height logarithmic, at the cost of a more complex implementation.

sections.heading: Recursion is the natural language
body: Most tree problems are one recursive call per subtree plus a combine step. State the base case, trust the recursion for the subtrees, and decide what information must flow upward. If two values must be returned, return a small struct or a pair rather than reaching for a global.
The classic trap is solving a subtree problem bottom-up while only tracking one value. Height, diameter, balance and largest-path-sum each need the subtree result plus a running best answer.

keyPoints: In-order on a BST yields sorted values
Balanced BST operations are O(log n); unbalanced degrades to O(n)
Deletion with two children uses the in-order successor
Recursion solves most tree problems; post-order fits bottom-up work
AVL and red-black keep height logarithmic automatically

examples.title: Validating a BST
examples.body: Instead of checking only parent and child, carry an allowed range down the recursion. Every node must lie strictly between a low and high bound, which catches violations several levels away.

examples.title: Tree diameter
examples.body: Return the height of each subtree while updating a global best with the sum of the two tallest child heights. The answer is the largest such sum, not the tree's height.

mistakes: Comparing only a node with its immediate children
Forgetting the empty tree base case
Building a BST from sorted input and getting a linked list
Recomputing subtree work instead of returning it once
practiceTip: Implement in-order traversal both recursively and with an explicit stack. The stack version is the same logic with the call stack made visible.

subject: ds
name: Heaps & Priority Queues
tagline: Always know the extreme, in O(log n)
summary: A binary heap keeps the smallest or largest element at the root. Insert and extract-min are O(log n), peek is O(1), and building a heap from n items is O(n). It is the structure behind priority queues, scheduling and every top-k problem.

sections.heading: The array-backed complete tree
body: A heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array: the children of index i live at 2i+1 and 2i+2, and the parent at (i-1)/2. That layout needs no pointers, which makes it compact and cache friendly.

Insertion appends and then sifts the new element up until the heap property holds. Extraction swaps the root with the last element, removes the tail, and sifts down. Both touch at most the height of the tree.
bullets: Min-heap: parent smaller than children, peek gives the minimum
Max-heap: the mirror image, used for top-k largest
Build-heap is O(n), not O(n log n)
Heap sort: n extractions, O(n log n), in place

sections.heading: The top-k and k-way merge patterns
body: For the k largest elements, keep a min-heap of size k: push everything, and whenever the size exceeds k pop the smallest. The heap then always holds the k largest seen so far, at O(n log k) instead of O(n log n) for a full sort.

K-way merging, such as merging k sorted lists, puts the head of each list in a heap and repeatedly pops the smallest and pushes its successor. Dijkstra's shortest path and Huffman coding are the same pattern over different domains.

keyPoints: Peek O(1), insert and extract O(log n), build O(n)
A min-heap of size k answers top-k largest in O(n log k)
K-way merge, Dijkstra and Huffman coding are heap patterns
Stored in an array with index arithmetic, no pointers
A heap does not give sorted iteration without extracting

examples.title: K closest points to the origin
examples.body: Keep a max-heap of size k keyed by distance. For each point, push and pop when the size exceeds k. What remains is the k closest, in O(n log k).

examples.title: Merging k sorted lists
examples.body: Push the first node of each list into a min-heap keyed by value. Pop the smallest, append it to the output, and push its successor. Total O(N log k) for N total nodes.

mistakes: Sorting when a heap of size k would do
Forgetting to update the key after changing a priority
Using a min-heap when the question asks for largest, or vice versa
Assuming a heap supports arbitrary search
practiceTip: Implement heapify, push and pop once from the array formulas. Afterwards every top-k problem is a two-line change.

subject: ds
name: Graphs
tagline: Nodes plus edges: the model for networks
summary: A graph is a set of vertices connected by edges, directed or undirected, weighted or not. It models anything with relationships, and nearly every graph problem is a traversal plus a bookkeeping decision about what to record along the way.

sections.heading: Representation drives the cost
body: An adjacency list stores, per vertex, the list of its neighbours: O(V + E) space, O(degree) to enumerate neighbours, which suits sparse graphs and is what almost every algorithm assumes. An adjacency matrix stores a V x V grid: O(V^2) space, O(1) edge test, which suits dense graphs and Floyd-Warshall style all-pairs work.
Choosing the wrong representation turns an O(V + E) traversal into an O(V^2) scan, which is the most common performance failure in graph code.
bullets: Adjacency list: sparse graphs, traversal, O(V + E)
Adjacency matrix: dense graphs, fast edge test, O(V^2)
Directed: one-way edges, indegree and outdegree differ
Weighted: carry distances or costs alongside neighbours

sections.heading: BFS, DFS and what each gives you
body: BFS with a queue explores in layers, so the first time it reaches a node it has found the shortest path in an unweighted graph. DFS with a stack or recursion explores as deep as possible, which is what you want for connectivity, cycle detection, topological order and component labelling.

Both need a visited set, and the set must be marked when a node is first discovered, not when it is finished. Marking late lets the same node enter the queue many times and turns a linear traversal into an exponential one.

sections.heading: The algorithm selection table
body: Shortest path with non-negative weights is Dijkstra with a heap. Negative weights call for Bellman-Ford. All pairs shortest paths call for Floyd-Warshall on small graphs. Minimum spanning tree is Prim with a heap or Kruskal with union-find. Ordering with dependencies is topological sort, which only exists on a directed acyclic graph.
Cycle detection differs by graph type: a back edge during DFS detects a cycle in a directed graph, while an undirected graph needs care to ignore the edge back to the immediate parent.

keyPoints: Adjacency list for sparse, matrix for dense; the choice changes the complexity
BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs
DFS gives connectivity, cycles and topological order
Mark visited on discovery, or the traversal blows up
Dijkstra for non-negative weights, Bellman-Ford for negatives, union-find for MST

examples.title: Course prerequisites
examples.body: Model courses as nodes and prerequisites as directed edges. If a topological order exists the schedule is possible; if a cycle is found it is not. Kahn's algorithm with indegree counts produces the order directly.

examples.title: Number of islands
examples.body: Treat the grid as a graph and flood-fill from each unvisited land cell with BFS or DFS, marking cells as visited. Each flood fill is one island, so the total cost is O(rows * cols).

mistakes: Marking visited when finishing instead of discovering
Choosing a matrix for a sparse graph and paying O(V^2)
Using Dijkstra with negative edge weights
Treating an undirected cycle check the same as a directed one
practiceTip: Write one generic traversal that takes a neighbour function and a visitor. Every graph algorithm after that is a different visitor.

subject: ds
name: Union-Find (Disjoint Sets)
tagline: Group things, answer 'are these connected' in near O(1)
summary: Union-find maintains a partition of elements into disjoint sets and answers two questions: which set does this element belong to, and are two elements in the same set. With path compression and union by rank both operations are effectively constant time.

sections.heading: Forests, not flat arrays
body: Each element points to a parent, and roots point to themselves. Find walks up to the root, and union attaches one root under the other. Without care the trees degenerate into chains and find becomes O(n).

Path compression makes every node on the find path point directly at the root, flattening the forest as you use it. Union by rank or size attaches the shorter tree under the taller one, which bounds the height. Together they give an amortised cost per operation of O(alpha(n)), which is under 5 for any realistic n.
bullets: Find with path compression: flatten while searching
Union by size or rank: never make the tall tree taller
Components in an undirected graph: union every edge, count roots
Kruskal's MST: sort edges, union endpoints, skip if already joined
Cycle detection in an undirected graph: an edge that unions two already-joined nodes is a cycle

sections.heading: Why it beats BFS here
body: Connectivity questions asked many times, in any order, with edges arriving incrementally, are exactly what union-find is for. BFS answers one connectivity query in O(V + E), which is wasteful when the same question is asked repeatedly.
The trade is that union-find cannot answer path questions or shortest paths, only membership. If you need the path itself, run BFS or DFS instead.

keyPoints: Two operations: find the set, and union two sets
Path compression plus union by rank make operations near O(1)
It answers membership, never paths or distances
Kruskal's MST and undirected cycle detection are the classic uses
It handles incremental edges without recomputation

examples.title: Redundant connection
examples.body: Process edges in order, unioning endpoints. The first edge whose endpoints are already in the same set closes a cycle, and that edge is the redundant one.

examples.title: Accounts merge
examples.body: Union accounts that share an email, then group accounts by their set's root. Path compression keeps the repeated finds cheap.

mistakes: Union without rank or size, which degrades to O(n) per find
Forgetting to compress the path on find
Expecting path or distance information from union-find
Assuming elements are 0..n-1 without a mapping from ids to indices
practiceTip: Implement both optimisations together. Implementing either alone is the usual reason a union-find solution times out.

subject: ds
name: Strings
tagline: Sequences with alphabets, windows and matching
summary: Strings are arrays of characters, so every array technique applies, plus a few of their own: sliding windows over characters, frequency counting with a fixed alphabet, and pattern matching where naive comparison is O(n*m).

sections.heading: The character-count toolkit
body: A fixed alphabet of 26 or 128 entries turns character comparisons into array lookups. Anagrams become equal frequency vectors. Permutation-in-string becomes a window whose frequency vector matches the pattern's. Palindromes become counts plus at most one odd entry.
This is the single most useful string trick: convert the problem into counts, then slide a window and compare vectors.
bullets: Frequency array of 26 for lowercase letters
Sliding window over the alphabet for substring problems
Two pointers from both ends for palindromes
Sort the characters to canonicalise anagrams

sections.heading: Matching without O(n*m)
body: Naive matching compares the pattern at every offset, costing O(n*m). Rolling hashes, as in Rabin-Karp, update the hash of the next window in O(1) and only compare fully on a hash hit, giving O(n + m) on average. The Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm precomputes a failure function so it never re-examines characters, achieving O(n + m) worst case.
For interview purposes, knowing that naive is O(n*m) and that hashing or a prefix function removes the factor of m is usually the whole answer.

keyPoints: Every array technique applies to strings
A fixed-size frequency array replaces nested character comparisons
Sliding windows handle substring and permutation questions in O(n)
Naive matching is O(n*m); hashing or KMP removes the factor
Two pointers from the ends handle palindromes

examples.title: Longest substring without repeating characters
examples.body: Expand a right pointer and store the last index of each character. When a repeat appears inside the window, jump the left pointer past the previous occurrence. One pass, O(n).

examples.title: Valid anagram
examples.body: Count characters of both strings in 26-element arrays and compare. O(n) time, O(1) space, no sorting needed.

mistakes: Building a new substring for every window instead of counting
Using O(n*m) matching when a hash would do
Case sensitivity and whitespace assumptions
Assuming a fixed alphabet when the input is Unicode
practiceTip: Whenever you write a nested loop over two strings, check whether a frequency array or a rolling hash collapses the inner loop.

subject: ds
name: Complexity Analysis
tagline: Big-O is a promise about growth, not seconds
summary: Big-O describes how cost grows with input size, ignoring constants and lower-order terms. It is the vocabulary for comparing algorithms, and getting it right requires counting the operations that actually repeat, including hidden ones inside library calls.

sections.heading: Reading complexity from code
body: Sequential statements add, nested loops multiply, and a loop that halves its range each step is logarithmic. A loop whose bound is reduced by a constant factor each iteration runs O(log n) times regardless of the factor, because constants disappear.
Recursion needs a different tool: write the recurrence, then expand it. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) is merge sort and solves to O(n log n); T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) is a linear recursion and solves to O(n^2).
bullets: Nested loops over the same data: multiply
Halving the input each step: O(log n)
Two independent recursions per call: often exponential
Amortised: spread occasional expensive operations over cheap ones
Space complexity counts memory beyond the input

sections.heading: Amortised, worst and best are different questions
body: Worst case is the guarantee, average case is the expectation, and amortised spreads a rare expensive operation across many cheap ones. A dynamic array append is worst case O(n) when it reallocates, but amortised O(1) because the reallocation happens after a doubling.
Quoting worst case for an amortised structure sounds wrong, and quoting amortised when someone asks for a guarantee is misleading. Say which one you mean.

sections.heading: The hidden costs
body: String concatenation in a loop, copying a container into a function parameter, and sorting inside a loop are the usual invisible O(n) or O(n log n) additions. Library calls are not free: check whether a lookup is a hash map or a linear scan.
Complexity also ignores cache behaviour, which is why an O(n) linked-list traversal can be slower in practice than an O(n log n) array sort for small n.

keyPoints: Sequential adds, nested multiplies, halving is logarithmic
Recursion needs a recurrence, expanded or guessed and proved
Amortised is not the same as worst case; say which you mean
Library calls can hide a linear scan
Constants and cache effects matter for small inputs

examples.title: Building a string in a loop
examples.body: Concatenating in a loop copies the growing prefix each time, giving O(n^2). Appending to a buffer, or collecting parts and joining once, is O(n).

examples.title: Two nested loops that are actually linear
examples.body: A left pointer that only moves forward inside an outer right-pointer loop executes O(2n) total, which is O(n). Not every nesting is quadratic; check whether the inner bound resets.

mistakes: Counting only the loop body and ignoring the bound's own cost
Calling an amortised structure's worst case O(1)
Forgetting that sorting is O(n log n)
Assuming a nested loop must be quadratic without checking the bounds
practiceTip: State the complexity of every function you write today, including the ones that call library functions. It takes seconds and catches real bugs.

subject: signals
name: Signals & Systems
tagline: Describe signals in time, then in frequency
summary: A signal is a function of time or of index, and a system maps input signals to output signals. The two domains, time and frequency, are equivalent views of the same information, and most analysis is about knowing which view makes a question easy.

sections.heading: Signals and their properties
body: A continuous-time signal is defined for every t; a discrete-time signal only at integer indices. Even signals satisfy x(t) = x(-t), odd signals satisfy x(t) = -x(-t), and any signal can be split into those two parts.

The unit impulse is the identity under convolution: convolving a signal with delta(n) returns the signal unchanged, and convolving with a shifted impulse shifts it. That single property is what makes impulse response a complete description of an LTI system.
bullets: Continuous versus discrete: defined for all t, or only at integers
Even and odd decompositions
Unit impulse is the identity for convolution
Energy signals have finite energy; power signals have finite average power

sections.heading: LTI systems
body: A system is linear if superposition holds, and time-invariant if a shifted input produces the same shifted output. Together they mean the system is completely described by its impulse response, and any input can be written as shifted impulses, so the output is the convolution of the input with that response.

This is why one experiment, measuring the impulse response, characterises the whole system. Stability is then a property of that response: for discrete-time BIBO stability it must be absolutely summable.

keyPoints: Continuous signals are defined for all t; discrete only at integers
