Convolution with a unit impulse returns the signal unchanged
An LTI system is fully described by its impulse response
Output equals input convolved with the impulse response
BIBO stability requires an absolutely summable impulse response

examples.title: Why the impulse response suffices
examples.body: Any input is a sum of shifted impulses. By superposition the output is the same sum of shifted impulse responses, which is exactly the convolution integral or sum.

examples.title: Checking stability
examples.body: For a discrete-time system, sum the absolute values of the impulse response. A finite sum means every bounded input produces a bounded output.

mistakes: Confusing continuous and discrete definitions
Assuming a system is LTI without checking time invariance
Treating energy and power signals interchangeably
Forgetting that convolution with delta shifts as well as scales
practiceTip: For each system you meet, state whether it is linear and time-invariant before doing anything else. Almost every later step depends on that answer.

subject: signals
name: Fourier Analysis & Sampling
tagline: Frequency content, and the rate needed to capture it
summary: The Fourier transform expresses a signal as a sum of sinusoids, which turns convolution into multiplication and filtering into attenuation. Sampling theory then states the rate needed to capture that content without loss.

sections.heading: The transform and its consequences
body: The Fourier transform converts between time and frequency. The most useful consequence is the duality of operations: convolution in one domain equals multiplication in the other, so filtering a signal is multiplying its spectrum, and modulating a signal is convolving its spectrum.
Properties are what make analysis fast: linearity, time shifting adding a linear phase, scaling in one domain inverting in the other, and Parseval's theorem relating energy across domains.
bullets: Convolution in time equals multiplication in frequency
A time shift adds a linear phase term
The transform of a real signal has conjugate symmetry
The DFT is the sampled version, computed by the FFT in O(n log n)

sections.heading: Sampling and aliasing
body: Sampling replicates the spectrum at multiples of the sampling rate. If the rate is above twice the highest frequency, the replicas do not overlap and the original can be recovered by an ideal low-pass filter. Below that rate, replicas overlap and high frequencies masquerade as low ones, which is aliasing.

Reconstruction uses the sinc interpolator, which is equivalent to ideal low-pass filtering. Quantisation adds a separate error, bounded by half a step, which is why resolution matters independently of rate.

keyPoints: The transform converts convolution to multiplication
A time shift only adds a linear phase term
Nyquist: sample above twice the bandwidth for perfect reconstruction
Aliasing is spectrum overlap from too low a rate
The FFT computes the DFT in O(n log n)

examples.title: Filtering by multiplication
examples.body: Instead of convolving a long signal with a filter, transform both, multiply the spectra and transform back. The cost is dominated by two FFTs rather than a long convolution.

examples.title: Aliasing in audio
examples.body: Sampling a 12 kHz tone at 16 kHz folds it to 4 kHz, an audible artefact. Anti-aliasing filters before the sampler prevent the fold.

mistakes: Sampling below Nyquist and expecting clean recovery
Confusing quantisation error with aliasing
Forgetting the linear phase term on time shifts
Assuming the FFT is exact for non-periodic signals
practiceTip: Compute the spectrum of a simple rectangular pulse by hand once. It makes every windowing discussion concrete.

subject: analog
name: Analog Circuits
tagline: Diodes, transistors and amplifiers from first principles
summary: Analog circuits process continuously varying signals with diodes, transistors and operational amplifiers. Almost every analysis reduces to a bias point, a small-signal model, and a check that the device stays in its intended region.

sections.heading: The three-step analysis
body: First find the DC operating point, because that determines gain and headroom. Second replace the active device with its small-signal model, which is a controlled source plus an output resistance. Third verify the small-signal assumptions still hold, meaning the device has not left its active region.
Skipping the operating point is the most common error, because gain depends on it directly, and a circuit that is fine on paper can be saturated in practice.
bullets: Diode: conducts one way, modelled as a voltage source plus resistance
BJT: current-controlled, exponential relationship
MOSFET: voltage-controlled, square-law in saturation
Op-amp: very high gain, used with feedback to set behaviour
Feedback trades gain for bandwidth and linearity

sections.heading: Feedback and stability
body: Negative feedback sets the closed-loop behaviour from passive components and makes the circuit insensitive to device variation. The price is reduced loop gain and the possibility of oscillation if the phase shift reaches 180 degrees while the loop gain is still above one.
Gain margin and phase margin quantify how close the circuit is to that condition. Compensating a circuit means deliberately reducing the gain at high frequency to buy back phase margin.

keyPoints: Find the DC operating point before any small-signal analysis
BJTs are current-controlled; MOSFETs are voltage-controlled
Op-amp behaviour is set by feedback, not by the device
Negative feedback buys linearity at the cost of gain
Gain and phase margin quantify stability

examples.title: Op-amp inverting amplifier
examples.body: With the input through a resistor to the inverting node and feedback from output to that node, the gain is set by the ratio of the two resistors and is almost independent of the op-amp's own gain.

examples.title: Why an amplifier oscillates
examples.body: A three-pole amplifier has enough phase shift to make negative feedback positive at high frequency. Adding a compensation capacitor pushes the dominant pole lower, restoring phase margin.

mistakes: Analysing small signal without the DC bias
Treating an op-amp's output as unlimited
Ignoring loading between cascaded stages
Assuming feedback always improves stability
practiceTip: For each amplifier stage you analyse, write the operating point, the small-signal model and the region check, in that order.

subject: hr
name: HR & Behavioural Interviews
tagline: Structured stories that show how you work
summary: Behavioural questions ask for evidence, not opinion. The strongest answers are short, specific stories with a clear situation, the decision you made, the action you took and the measurable result.

sections.heading: STAR is the shape, not a script
body: Situation gives enough context to make the story make sense. Task states what was yours to do. Action is the bulk, describing what you specifically did. Result states the outcome, with numbers where they exist.
Most answers fail by spending eighty percent of the time on situation. Keep it to two sentences and let action carry the story, because that is what the interviewer is assessing.
bullets: Two sentences of situation, no more
Use 'I' for what you did, 'we' for the team context
Quantify the result: time, cost, error rate, revenue
One story can serve several questions if you vary the emphasis
Prepare three stories that cover conflict, failure and impact

sections.heading: Answer the question actually asked
body: Interviewers listen for whether the story matches the question. A conflict question answered with a success story reads as avoidance, however impressive the achievement.
When asked about a failure, the expected shape is: what went wrong, what you did about it, and what you changed afterwards. Skipping the last part is what most candidates get wrong.

keyPoints: Situation short, action detailed, result quantified
Be honest about your own contribution within the team
Match the story to the question asked
For failure questions, always end with what changed
Three prepared stories cover most interviews

examples.title: A conflict question
examples.body: Situation: two engineers disagreed on an API shape. Task: I owned the interface. Action: I listed the constraints each design protected and proposed a third design satisfying both. Result: adopted, and the disputed point never had to be revisited.

examples.title: A failure question
examples.body: Situation: I shipped a change that broke a downstream consumer. Action: I rolled back immediately, notified the team, added the missing integration test. Result: no recurrence in the following quarter, and the rollback checklist is now standard.

mistakes: Describing the team's work as if it were yours
Answering a failure question with a success story
Leaving out the result
Reciting a memorised paragraph that does not fit the question
practiceTip: Write three stories in STAR form and read them aloud. Anything that takes longer than ninety seconds is too long.

subject: hr
name: Situational & Workplace Questions
tagline: Show judgement under a hypothetical constraint
summary: Situational questions pose a hypothetical conflict, such as an impossible deadline or a disagreement with a manager. They are assessing judgement and self-awareness, and the best answers name the trade-off before choosing.

sections.heading: Name the tension, then decide
body: Almost every situational question hides a genuine tension: quality against speed, honesty against harmony, individual work against team goals. Saying what the tension is demonstrates that you understood the question.
Then commit to an answer. Waffling between options is read as indecision, and hedging with 'it depends' without saying what it depends on is worse than a wrong choice.
bullets: State the trade-off you see
Give a first action, not a whole philosophy
Mention what information would change your mind
Prefer honest, early communication over quiet absorption

sections.heading: Questions about you
body: Strengths should be evidenced, not asserted: name the strength and the story that proves it. Weaknesses should be real, containable and improving, never a disguised strength.
'Where do you see yourself in five years' is asking whether your goals match the role. Align your answer with what the job actually offers.

keyPoints: Name the trade-off before choosing
Commit to an answer rather than hedging
Evidences strengths; weaknesses should be real and improving
Prefer early honest communication to quiet absorption
Match your goals answer to what the role offers

examples.title: An impossible deadline
examples.body: The tension is scope against date. I would confirm what must ship, cut or defer the rest explicitly, and tell stakeholders which items moved and when they land. I would not silently deliver partial work on all fronts.

examples.title: Disagreeing with your manager
examples.body: I would ask what outcome they are optimising for, present the evidence for my concern once, and commit to their decision while recording the risk. Escalating immediately or ignoring the decision are both wrong.

mistakes: Answering with a philosophy instead of a first action
Claiming a weakness that is obviously a strength
Hedging so much that no position is taken
Ignoring the trade-off the question is really testing
practiceTip: Answer every situational question in three sentences: the tension, your first action, and what would change your mind.

subject: networks
name: Computer Networks
tagline: Layers, because no single problem is tractable at once
summary: Networking is organised in layers, each solving one problem and offering a service to the one above. Most confusion in networking interviews comes from mixing concerns that belong to different layers.

sections.heading: The layers and their jobs
body: The physical layer moves bits. The data link layer moves frames between directly connected nodes and handles local addressing. The network layer routes packets end to end across many hops. The transport layer delivers data between processes, with reliability if required. The application layer carries the protocol of the actual program.
TCP/IP collapses the OSI model's session and presentation layers into the application layer, which is why the two models never quite line up.
bullets: IP: addressing and routing, best effort, no delivery guarantee
TCP: reliable, ordered, connection-oriented byte stream
UDP: unreliable, unordered, but cheap and connectionless
ARP: maps IP addresses to local MAC addresses
DNS: resolves names to addresses

sections.heading: Reliability is a layer decision
body: TCP adds sequence numbers, acknowledgements, retransmission and flow control, which is why a lost packet is invisible to the application. UDP adds none of that, so loss, duplication and reordering are the application's problem.
Choosing UDP is usually about latency or multicast, not about simplicity. Video calls, DNS queries and game state tolerate some loss far better than they tolerate the delay of retransmission.

keyPoints: Each layer solves one problem for the layer above
IP routes but does not guarantee delivery
TCP is reliable and ordered; UDP is neither but is cheap
ARP resolves local addresses; DNS resolves names
The OSI and TCP/IP models differ in the upper layers

examples.title: Why a video call uses UDP
examples.body: Retransmitting a dropped video frame arrives too late to display. Dropping it keeps latency low and the picture slightly degraded, which is the better trade.

examples.title: Why a file download uses TCP
examples.body: Every byte must arrive exactly once and in order, so retransmission and reordering are worth their cost. Reliability is the point.

mistakes: Expecting IP to guarantee delivery
Using TCP where per-packet latency dominates
Confusing MAC addresses with IP addresses
Attributing flow control to the network layer
practiceTip: For each protocol you meet, name its layer and the problem it solves. Layer confusion causes most wrong answers.

subject: networks
name: TCP, UDP & Congestion Control
tagline: Reliability, and sharing a link without collapsing it
summary: TCP provides a reliable ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmission, and controls its rate to avoid overwhelming the network. Congestion control is what keeps a shared link from collapsing.

sections.heading: How TCP builds reliability
body: Every byte is numbered. The receiver acknowledges what it has received contiguously, and the sender retransmits anything unacknowledged after a timeout, or faster on duplicate acknowledgements. A sliding window lets many segments be in flight, bounded by both the receiver's buffer and the sender's congestion window.
The three-way handshake establishes initial sequence numbers on both sides, and the four-way teardown closes each direction independently because a connection is bidirectional.
bullets: Sequence numbers order and de-duplicate bytes
Cumulative ACKs identify the contiguous prefix received
Sliding window bounds bytes in flight
Flow control uses the receiver's advertised window
Congestion control uses the sender's estimated capacity

sections.heading: Congestion control
body: Slow start grows the congestion window exponentially until a threshold, then switches to congestion avoidance, growing linearly. A loss is treated as a signal of congestion: a timeout cuts the window hard, while duplicate acknowledgements trigger fast retransmit and fast recovery, which is gentler.
Additive increase, multiplicative decrease is the core idea: probe upward slowly, back off sharply. Modern variants add explicit congestion notification and delay-based estimation.

sections.heading: UDP, and when it is right
body: UDP adds only ports and a checksum. There is no connection, no ordering and no retransmission, so an application that needs those builds them selectively. QUIC does exactly this on top of UDP, adding stream multiplexing and encryption.
The choice is about which failures you can tolerate. A lost measurement in a sensor stream is ignorable; a lost byte in a firmware image is not.

keyPoints: TCP numbers bytes and retransmits what is not acknowledged
Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects the network
Slow start then congestion avoidance, with AIMD on loss
A timeout is treated more harshly than duplicate ACKs
UDP is cheaper and leaves reliability to the application

examples.title: Slow start in practice
examples.body: A new connection doubles its window each round trip until the first loss or the threshold, then grows linearly. That is why a fresh connection ramps rather than starting at full speed.

examples.title: Why QUIC exists
examples.body: TCP's head-of-line blocking stalls all streams when one packet is lost. QUIC runs independent streams over UDP, so one lost packet only delays the stream that needed it.

mistakes: Confusing flow control with congestion control
Assuming UDP guarantees ordering
Treating a timeout and duplicate ACKs identically
Building reliability by hand where TCP already provides it
practiceTip: Draw the slow-start curve for a connection that loses a packet at round trip five. It is the fastest way to internalise AIMD.

subject: networks
name: Routing
tagline: Finding a path through a network you do not control
summary: Routing decides which path packets take across a network of independently administered domains. Interior protocols find paths within one domain; exterior protocols decide between domains.

sections.heading: Interior versus exterior
body: Distance-vector protocols such as RIP have each router advertise the distance to every destination it knows, and neighbours trust those numbers. They are simple but converge slowly and can count to infinity. Link-state protocols such as OSPF have every router flood a description of its own links, so each router builds a full map and runs Dijkstra locally.

Convergence is the property that matters: how quickly all routers agree after a change. Link-state converges faster because each router has the whole picture, at the cost of more memory and message volume.
bullets: Distance vector: trust neighbours, simple, slow convergence
Link state: full topology, run Dijkstra, fast convergence
BGP: policy-based routing between autonomous systems
Count-to-infinity is a distance-vector failure mode
Hop count is a poor metric; cost reflects real capacity

sections.heading: BGP is policy, not shortest path
body: Between autonomous systems, the shortest path is rarely the right one. Business relationships, transit costs and regulations dominate, so BGP propagates reachability plus attributes and applies local policy at each hop.
That is why the internet does not route by latency. It routes by agreements, and an outage can propagate as a withdrawal of reachable prefixes.

keyPoints: Distance vector trusts neighbours; link state floods topology
Link state converges faster at higher memory and message cost
Count-to-infinity is specific to distance vector
BGP routes between domains by policy, not by distance
Hop count is a weak cost metric

examples.title: A link failure under OSPF
examples.body: The detecting router floods a new link-state advertisement. Every router recomputes shortest paths from the updated map, so all of them agree without waiting for numbers to propagate hop by hop.

examples.title: BGP route withdrawal
examples.body: When a network withdraws its prefix, that withdrawal propagates and routers remove the path. Until it converges, some traffic may be black-holed, which is the usual shape of an internet outage.

mistakes: Claiming the internet routes by shortest path
Confusing interior and exterior protocols
Assuming distance vector converges quickly
Using hop count as a real cost measure
practiceTip: Explain one failure mode for each family: count-to-infinity for distance vector, database size for link state.

subject: networks
name: DNS & the Application Layer
tagline: Names to addresses, then protocols on top
summary: DNS translates human-readable names into addresses through a hierarchy of delegated zones. Application protocols, HTTP, TLS, email and DNS itself, then run over the transport layer on top of that resolution.

sections.heading: How resolution works
body: A resolver asks a root server, which points to the top-level domain server, which points to the authoritative server for the zone, which returns the record. Each answer is cached with a time to live, which is why propagation is governed by TTLs rather than by any central authority.

A recursive resolver does the walking on the client's behalf; an iterative resolver returns referrals. The difference matters when debugging, because a recursive resolver's cache hides what the authoritative answer actually is.
bullets: A record: name to IPv4 address
AAAA record: name to IPv6 address
CNAME: alias to another name
MX: mail exchange for a domain
TTL: how long an answer may be cached

sections.heading: Application protocols over TCP
body: HTTP is a request-response protocol over TCP, now almost always wrapped in TLS. HTTP/1.1 reuses one connection but still has head-of-line blocking; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one connection; HTTP/3 moves to QUIC over UDP to remove that blocking entirely.
TLS sits between the application and transport, providing confidentiality and authentication, and its handshake cost is why session resumption and 0-RTT matter in practice.

keyPoints: DNS resolves names through delegated zones with cached answers
TTL governs how long a change takes to propagate
Recursive resolvers hide the authoritative answer in their cache
HTTP versions differ mainly in multiplexing and blocking
TLS provides confidentiality and authentication above TCP

examples.title: A change that takes too long
examples.body: A DNS record changed but clients still see the old address because resolvers cached the previous answer with a long TTL. Lowering the TTL before the change is the standard fix.

examples.title: HTTP/2 head-of-line blocking
examples.body: One lost TCP packet stalls every multiplexed stream because TCP delivers bytes in order. HTTP/3 over QUIC gives each stream independent delivery.

mistakes: Assuming DNS changes are instant
Confusing CNAME with A records at the zone apex
Treating TLS as a transport protocol
Expecting HTTP/2 to remove all head-of-line blocking
practiceTip: Trace a DNS resolution by hand for a name you know, naming the server at each step and what it returns.

subject: oop
name: Object-Oriented Programming
tagline: Bundle data with the operations that own it
summary: Object-oriented programming groups state and the operations valid on that state into a single unit, and restricts how outside code can touch it. The goal is that invariants are enforced in one place instead of being defended everywhere.

sections.heading: The four pillars, in plain terms
body: Encapsulation hides internals behind an interface so the invariants can be checked in one place. Abstraction exposes what an object does, not how. Inheritance reuses structure and behaviour along an is-a relationship. Polymorphism lets one interface dispatch to different implementations at runtime.
The measure of success is not the class count. It is whether a change to a rule requires editing one place or many.
bullets: Encapsulation: private state, public contract
Abstraction: what, not how
Inheritance: is-a, use sparingly
Polymorphism: virtual dispatch through a base pointer or reference
Composition: has-a, prefer it over inheritance when unsure

sections.heading: Design principles that actually change code
body: SOLID is the usual list. In practice three of them matter most: a class should have one reason to change, a module should be open for extension but closed for modification, and depend on abstractions rather than concrete classes.
Composition over inheritance is the pragmatic default. Inheritance is the tightest coupling available, so it should express a genuine subtype relationship, not code reuse.

keyPoints: Encapsulation protects invariants in exactly one place
Abstraction is the contract; the implementation is free to change
Prefer composition over inheritance unless it is a true subtype
Virtual functions give runtime polymorphism through a base reference
One reason to change is the most useful single heuristic

examples.title: Replacing inheritance with composition
examples.body: A Stack that inherits from Vector exposes push_back and leaks the underlying representation. Holding a Vector privately and exposing only push, pop and top keeps the contract tight.

examples.title: One reason to change
examples.body: A class that both computes scores and writes them to a database has two reasons to change: the formula and the storage. Splitting them means a database change never touches scoring logic.

mistakes: Using inheritance purely to reuse code
Public data members that let callers break invariants
Deep hierarchies that are hard to test in isolation
Adding getters and setters for every field, which is a struct with extra steps
practiceTip: For each class you write, name its single reason to change in one sentence. If you cannot, the class is doing two jobs.

subject: oop
name: Inheritance & Polymorphism
tagline: Substitutability is the contract, not the syntax
summary: Inheritance models is-a relationships; polymorphism makes a base reference or pointer dispatch to the derived implementation. Both are only correct when the derived type can genuinely substitute for the base.

sections.heading: What a virtual function costs and buys
body: A non-virtual call is resolved at compile time and can be inlined. A virtual call goes through a vtable pointer, one extra indirection, which blocks inlining and costs a small constant. That is cheap, and it buys the ability to run code that was written before the derived type existed.
A virtual destructor on a base class is not optional when deleting through a base pointer. Without it, the derived destructor never runs and resources leak.
bullets: Override means replacing, not overload; the signature must match
Mark overrides explicitly so a signature mismatch is a compile error
A virtual destructor on a polymorphic base is mandatory
Prefer private inheritance for implementation reuse, public for subtypes

sections.heading: Substitutability, not syntax
body: If a derived class strengthens the base's preconditions or weakens its postconditions, callers who worked with the base will break. That is the Liskov substitution violation, and it is the real reason inheritance hierarchies rot.
The practical test: can every function that accepts the base accept the derived without changing its behaviour? If not, inheritance is the wrong relationship.

keyPoints: Public inheritance means the derived is a substitutable base
Virtual calls cost one indirection and block inlining
A polymorphic base needs a virtual destructor
Strengthening preconditions breaks substitutability
Prefer composition unless the subtype relationship is real

examples.title: The square-rectangle trap
examples.body: A Square that inherits Rectangle must override setWidth to also set height, which changes the base's behaviour. Every consumer of Rectangle that assumes width and height are independent now behaves differently.

examples.title: Missing virtual destructor
examples.body: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer with a non-virtual destructor runs only the base destructor. The leak is deterministic and silent until it is not.

mistakes: Forgetting the virtual destructor on a polymorphic base
Similar signatures that silently overload instead of override
Using inheritance where composition would decouple the classes
Deep hierarchies where a flat design would be simpler
practiceTip: When reaching for inheritance, ask whether a base pointer to the derived really gets used somewhere. If nothing calls through the base, polymorphism is not buying anything.

subject: oop
name: Design Patterns & SOLID
tagline: Named solutions to recurring design pressure
summary: Design patterns are reusable answers to recurring design problems, and SOLID is the set of principles that tell you when you are drifting toward one. The value is the vocabulary: it lets you name the pressure before adding structure.

sections.heading: The patterns that pay for themselves
body: Strategy extracts an interchangeable algorithm behind an interface, which is how you avoid switch statements that grow. Factory hides construction so callers depend on the interface rather than the concrete type. Observer decouples a subject from its listeners. Repository separates domain logic from storage. Builder handles construction with many optional parts.
The warning sign that you need one is usually a change that ripples: adding a variant touches five files, or adding a storage backend forces edits throughout the domain.
bullets: Strategy: interchangeable behaviour behind one interface
Factory: construct without naming the concrete type
Observer: notify without knowing the listeners
Repository: domain logic independent of storage
Builder: many optional parts, readable construction
Singleton: one shared instance, but a global in disguise

sections.heading: SOLID as a checklist
body: One responsibility per class. Open for extension, closed for modification. Subtypes must be substitutable. Clients should depend on narrow interfaces. Depend on abstractions, not concretions.
These are heuristics, not laws. Applied rigidly they produce interfaces for every class, which is its own failure mode. Apply them at the seams where change actually happens.

keyPoints: Patterns are vocabulary for recurring design pressure
Strategy removes algorithm selection switches
Factory and Repository decouple creation and storage
SOLID is a checklist, not a mandate for every class
Apply structure at the seams where change happens

examples.title: Replacing a growing switch
examples.body: Each case becomes a Strategy implementing one interface, and the switch becomes a lookup in a factory map. Adding a variant is then a new file, not an edit to an existing one.

examples.title: Repository seam
examples.body: Business logic that reads and writes files directly cannot be tested without files. Passing in a repository interface lets tests supply an in-memory implementation.

mistakes: Applying a pattern because it is familiar, not because pressure exists
Building a hierarchy of abstract classes with one implementation each
Using a singleton where dependency injection would do
Refactoring toward a pattern before the requirement is real
practiceTip: Name the pressure first: which change is expensive today? Then pick the pattern that removes that specific cost.

subject: cpp_oop
name: C++ Templates & STL
tagline: Generic code, checked at compile time
summary: Templates let one function or class work with any type that supports the required operations. The compiler generates a separate instantiation per type, which gives zero runtime cost but larger binaries and long error messages.

sections.heading: What templates buy and cost
body: A template is a pattern the compiler stamps out per type, so type errors surface at compile time and there is no virtual dispatch or boxing. The price is code bloat, longer compile times, and errors that point deep into instantiated headers.

Writing templates means programming against an implicit interface, the operations you actually use, rather than a base class. That is powerful and unenforceable, so keep the required interface small and documented.
bullets: Templates are checked at compile time, with no runtime overhead
Concepts or static_assert can document the required operations
Prefer algorithms over inheritance for generic reuse
STL: vector, unordered_map, map, set, priority_queue, deque
Use emplace and reserve where the cost is measurable

sections.heading: The STL container choice
body: vector for almost everything: contiguous, cache friendly, amortised O(1) push_back. unordered_map and unordered_set for hashed lookup. map and set when you need ordered iteration. deque for cheap front insertion. priority_queue for heap behaviour.
The common mistake is using map where unordered_map would do, paying O(log n) and a heap allocation per node, or using list where vector would be faster despite the asymptotics.

keyPoints: Templates compile per type: fast, but bigger binaries
Errors point into instantiations, so keep required interfaces minimal
vector is the default container
unordered_map for lookup, map for ordered iteration
Prefer STL algorithms over hand-written loops

examples.title: One sort, many containers
examples.body: Because standard algorithms work on iterators, the same sort call works on vector, deque and array. The interface is the iterator, not the container.

examples.title: Choosing the map
examples.body: A config lookup that is read constantly needs unordered_map. A report that is iterated in key order needs map. The access pattern decides, not the name.

mistakes: Using map where unordered_map is faster
Using list for sequential access, losing cache locality
Over-templating code with one concrete call site
Ignoring reserve and emplace in hot paths
practiceTip: For each container you use, write the access pattern it serves. If you cannot, you probably chose the wrong one.

subject: os
name: Operating Systems
tagline: The referee between programs, memory and devices
summary: An operating system multiplexes the CPU, memory and devices between competing programs, giving each the illusion of a private machine. Nearly every OS concept follows from one of three resources: time, space, or hardware access.

sections.heading: The three ideas underneath everything
body: Processes are programs in execution, each with its own address space, so isolation is the default. Threads are the unit of scheduling within a process, sharing that address space, so communication is cheap and data races are possible. Virtual memory gives each process its own address space, backed by physical memory and disk.
Everything else, scheduling, synchronisation, paging, file systems, is a policy decision about how to share one of those three resources fairly and efficiently.
bullets: Process: isolation, its own memory, expensive to switch
Thread: shared memory, cheap to switch, needs synchronisation
Virtual memory: private address space, paging and swapping
System call: the only legitimate door into the kernel
Interrupt: how devices get the CPU's attention

sections.heading: Where the cost actually is
body: A context switch saves and restores registers and changes the address space, and on a process switch the TLB must be flushed, so switching is not free. A page fault costs a disk access. A syscall costs a mode switch.

Being able to name the cost is what separates a hand-wave from an answer. "A process switch is more expensive than a thread switch because the address space and TLB change" is the shape of a good reply.

keyPoints: Processes own memory; threads share it
Virtual memory gives isolation and allows overcommitment
Context switches, page faults and syscalls all have real costs
Synchronisation exists because threads share memory
Most OS policy is a fairness and throughput trade

examples.title: Process versus thread for a downloader
examples.body: Threads share memory so chunks are shared trivially, but need a mutex around shared state. Processes need IPC to share progress, so the extra isolation is rarely worth it here.

examples.title: Why a thread switch is cheaper
examples.body: Both save and restore registers, but a thread switch keeps the same address space, so it avoids changing the page table base and flushing the TLB.

mistakes: Confusing a process with a thread when discussing cost
Assuming threads need no synchronisation because they are fast
Treating virtual memory as unlimited physical memory
Forgetting that the kernel is not preemptible everywhere
practiceTip: For each OS topic below, write the one resource it manages: time, space or device access. The rest of the answer follows.

subject: os
name: Processes & Threads
tagline: Isolation versus sharing, and the states between
summary: A process is a program in execution with its own address space; a thread is a schedulable unit inside one. Processes cost more to create and switch but are isolated; threads are cheap but must coordinate explicitly.

sections.heading: Process states and transitions
body: A process moves between new, ready, running, waiting and terminated. It leaves the CPU either by yielding or being preempted, going to ready, or by needing to wait for I/O, going to waiting. Only the scheduler moves it back to running.

The PCB, or process control block, holds the state needed to resume: registers, memory map, open files and scheduling information. The size of that record is why switching processes costs more than switching threads.
bullets: fork creates a child with a copy of the parent's address space
Copy-on-write shares pages until one side writes
exec replaces the address space with a new program
Zombie: a finished child whose exit status was never collected
Orphan: a child whose parent exited, reparented to init

sections.heading: Threads: user versus kernel
body: User-level threads are managed by a library, so switching avoids the kernel but a blocking system call blocks the whole process. Kernel threads are scheduled by the OS, so one can block without stopping the others, at the cost of a kernel transition per switch.
Most modern runtimes map user threads onto kernel threads, which is why a blocking call no longer stalls an entire process the way it once did.

keyPoints: A process owns memory; a thread shares it
The PCB is what makes a process resumable
fork plus copy-on-write avoids copying memory until it is written
User threads switch cheaply; kernel threads block independently
Zombies are unreaped children, orphans are reparented children

examples.title: A web server with ten clients
examples.body: Ten threads in one process share the listening socket and in-memory state, needing a mutex only around the connection table. Ten processes would need shared memory or a socket handoff for the same job.

examples.title: Copy-on-write in fork
examples.body: fork marks both address spaces copy-on-write, so the child shares the parent's pages until either writes. A fork that immediately exec pays almost nothing for the copy.

mistakes: Calling a heavy computation a 'thread' without mentioning memory sharing
Assuming fork copies all physical memory
Using threads for isolation instead of processes
Forgetting to reap child processes
practiceTip: Write the process state diagram from memory, including the I/O wait transition that most people forget.

subject: os
name: CPU Scheduling
tagline: Whose turn is it, and what does that optimise
summary: The scheduler decides which ready process runs next. Every algorithm optimises something, throughput, response time or fairness, and every one can be derived from a simple rule applied to arrival and burst times.

sections.heading: The classic algorithms and their costs
body: FCFS runs in arrival order, is trivially fair in ordering, and suffers the convoy effect where short jobs wait behind long ones. SJF picks the shortest next burst and minimises average waiting time, but starves long jobs and requires knowing the future. Round Robin gives each process a fixed time slice, giving good response time at the cost of more switching.

Priority scheduling runs the highest priority first and can starve low priorities unless ageing is added. Multilevel feedback queue approximates SJF without knowing burst times by demoting jobs that use their whole slice.
bullets: FCFS: simple, convoy effect
SJF: optimal average wait, starves long jobs
Round Robin: good response, switching overhead
Priority: starvation without ageing
MLFQ: learns from behaviour, no burst estimates needed

sections.heading: Why MLFQ works
body: Jobs that block frequently for I/O yield the CPU before their slice ends and stay at high priority. CPU-bound jobs use the whole slice and are demoted. Over time interactive work floats up and batch work sinks, which is exactly the SJF preference, learned from observed behaviour.
Ageing prevents starvation: a job that waits too long is boosted. Modern schedulers extend this with latency targets rather than fixed slices.

keyPoints: Every algorithm optimises a different metric
SJF minimises average waiting time but starves long jobs
Round Robin buys response time with switching overhead
Priority scheduling needs ageing to avoid starvation
MLFQ approximates SJF by promoting interactive jobs

examples.title: Convoy effect under FCFS
examples.body: One CPU-bound job arrives first while twenty I/O-bound jobs queue behind it, so the I/O devices idle and response time collapses. Shortest-job-first or round robin would interleave them.

examples.title: Starving under priority
examples.body: A steady stream of high-priority jobs prevents a low-priority job from ever running. Ageing, raising priority with waiting time, fixes it without changing the ordering rule.

mistakes: Claiming SJF is starvation-free
Forgetting switching overhead when comparing quanta
Assuming burst times are known in a real scheduler
Confusing waiting time with turnaround time
practiceTip: Compute average waiting time by hand for FCFS, SJF and Round Robin on the same three-process trace. The numbers make the trade-offs obvious.

subject: os
name: Synchronisation & Deadlock
tagline: Making concurrent access correct, then making it not deadlock
summary: When threads share state, mutual exclusion is required for correctness, and that exclusion introduces the possibility of deadlock. The subject is two problems in sequence: exclude correctly, then avoid the failure modes exclusion creates.

sections.heading: Mutual exclusion and its primitives
body: A correct solution to the critical section problem needs mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting. Mutexes provide mutual exclusion with ownership, so only the locking thread may unlock. Semaphores are counters usable for exclusion or signalling, and can be signalled by a different thread than the one that waited.

A monitor combines a mutex with condition variables, so wait and signal happen atomically with respect to the lock. Monitors are what most languages expose, and they remove the classic lost-wakeup bug when used properly.
bullets: Mutex: ownership, exclusion
Semaphore: counting, signalling across threads
Condition variable: wait and notify under a lock
Atomic: lock-free operations for single values
Read-write lock: many readers or one writer

sections.heading: Deadlock and the four Coffman conditions
body: Deadlock requires mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait to hold simultaneously. Prevention attacks one condition: require all locks up front, allow preemption, or impose a total lock ordering. Avoidance, as in the banker's algorithm, checks whether a request keeps the system in a safe state before granting it.
The lock hierarchy is the practical fix. If every thread acquires locks in a globally agreed order, circular wait becomes impossible, and no runtime machinery is needed.

sections.heading: Liveness beyond deadlock
body: Starvation is a fairness failure: a thread never gets the resource because others keep winning. Livelock is worse in a way: threads keep reacting to each other and make no progress. Priority inversion, where a high-priority thread waits behind a low one holding its lock, is a classic real-world case fixed by priority inheritance.
Naming these precisely is what distinguishes an answer from a description.

keyPoints: Critical section solutions need exclusion, progress and bounded waiting
Mutex has ownership; semaphore counts and signals
Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions at once
A global lock ordering removes circular wait cheaply
Starvation, livelock and priority inversion are distinct failures

examples.title: Lock hierarchy preventing deadlock
examples.body: Two threads both need locks A and B. Agreeing that A is always taken first makes circular wait impossible, and the code needs no timeout or detection machinery.

examples.title: Priority inheritance
examples.body: A medium-priority task runs while a high-priority one blocks on a lock held by a low-priority task. Letting the low task inherit the high priority lets it finish and release the lock, unblocking the high one.

mistakes: Using a mutex where signalling across threads was needed
Holding a lock across a blocking call
Acquiring locks in inconsistent order across functions
Confusing starvation with deadlock
practiceTip: Write the readers-writers problem with writer priority, then explain which thread starves and why. That single exercise covers exclusion, fairness and starvation.

subject: os
name: Memory & Virtual Memory
tagline: Private address spaces, backed by pages
summary: Virtual memory gives every process a private address space mapped onto physical frames and backing store. Paging implements it in fixed-size units, which simplifies allocation at the cost of a translation step on every access.

sections.heading: Translation and the TLB
body: A virtual address is split into a page number and an offset. The page number indexes the page table to produce a frame number, and the offset is appended. A TLB miss is not automatically a page fault: the translation may simply be uncached, and the page table in memory supplies it.
Because the page table base register changes on every process switch, the TLB must be flushed or tagged, which is a real cost of context switching.
bullets: A TLB miss means the cached translation is absent
A page fault means the page is not resident
Effective access time blends hit and miss rates
Multi-level tables trade memory for lookup depth
Copy-on-write avoids copying on fork

sections.heading: Replacement and working sets
body: When a page must be evicted, the OS picks by some policy: FIFO, optimal, LRU or clock. LRU approximates optimal well and is implemented approximately with reference bits. Belady's anomaly, where more frames cause more faults, can happen with FIFO.

Thrashing occurs when the total working set exceeds physical memory, and the system spends its time servicing faults instead of running programs. The fix is to reduce the degree of multiprogramming, which is what working-set and page-fault-frequency models do.

keyPoints: Virtual addresses are translated per access; the TLB caches that
A TLB miss is not a page fault
Effective access time depends on the fault rate
LRU approximates optimal replacement; FIFO can show Belady's anomaly
Thrashing is a working-set problem, fixed by reducing concurrency

examples.title: Demand paging
examples.body: Pages are loaded only on first access, so a large program's startup touches only the pages it uses. The cost is a fault per newly touched page, which demand paging spreads across execution.

examples.title: Fork without copying
examples.body: fork marks the shared pages copy-on-write. The child's first write to a page triggers a fault that copies just that page, so a fork followed by exec costs almost no copying.

mistakes: Treating a TLB miss as a page fault
Claiming more frames always reduce faults
Ignoring that the page table walk costs extra memory accesses
Forgetting the TLB flush cost on context switch
practiceTip: Compute effective access time for a given page-fault rate, then explain what changes if the fault rate doubles.

subject: communication
name: Communication Skills
tagline: Say less, be understood more
summary: Communication is the transfer of intent, not the delivery of words. Strong communicators tailor the message to the listener, choose the right channel, and confirm that meaning landed before moving on.

sections.heading: Clarity beats completeness
body: Most miscommunication comes from dumping everything you know instead of the one thing the listener needs. Before you speak, decide the single takeaway: if the listener remembers only one sentence, which one should it be?
Structure helps. Lead with the conclusion, then the reason, then the detail. Interviewers and managers are busy; they reward people who get to the point and stay there.
bullets: One idea per sentence, one decision per message
Name the ask explicitly: decide, review, or just be aware
Replace jargon with the plain word unless the jargon is shared

sections.heading: Listening is the active half
body: Listening is not waiting for your turn to talk. It is testing your understanding against what the other person actually said, and asking when the two disagree.
Paraphrase the point back in your own words before you respond. It costs ten seconds and prevents the most expensive class of meeting failure: two people solving different problems.
bullets: Ask what outcome the other person wants before proposing one
Silence after a question is a tool, not a gap to fill
Note the emotional signal as carefully as the factual one

sections.heading: Pick the channel on purpose
body: Chat is for facts, calls are for nuance, documents are for anything that must be agreed later. Sending nuance over chat is the fastest way to turn a five-minute conversation into a three-day thread.
Written communication has a half-life: anything you send will be read by someone who lacks your context. Write for that reader, not for the person who already knows.

keyPoints: Decide the single takeaway before you open your mouth
Conclusion first, then reasoning, then supporting detail
Paraphrase before you reply to confirm you understood
Match the channel to the ambiguity of the message
Write for the reader who lacks your context

examples.title: Explaining a delay
examples.body: Instead of narrating every hour lost, say what slipped, by how much, what you are doing about it, and what you need from them. Four sentences, no defensiveness.

examples.title: Answering a vague request
examples.body: When someone asks you to 'look into something', reply with the three possible interpretations and ask which one they meant. That converts a guessing game into a thirty-second clarification.

mistakes: Burying the request at the end of a long explanation
Assuming silence means agreement
Using channel-inappropriate detail, such as a policy argument in a chat window
Correcting someone's wording instead of engaging their point
practiceTip: Practice by explaining one technical concept per day to a non-technical friend in under two minutes, with no slides.

subject: teamwork
name: Teamwork & Collaboration
tagline: Make the people around you more effective
summary: Teams fail on coordination long before they fail on skill. Good collaborators reduce the work other people need to do, share context before it is needed, and treat disagreement as information rather than a contest.

sections.heading: Reduce other people's cost
body: The measurable form of teamwork is friction: how much effort does someone need to work with you? Reliable handoffs, honest status, and readable work products all lower that number.
When you finish something, ask who will touch it next and what they will need. Writing that down takes minutes and saves them an hour.
bullets: Hand off with context: goal, state, next step, known risks
Surface blockers early; a surprise delay is worse than the delay
Leave the codebase and the meeting notes better than you found them

sections.heading: Disagree with the work, not the person
body: Healthy teams separate the idea from the identity of whoever proposed it. Critique the artifact: which assumption is weakest, which evidence would change your mind?
Say what you would need to be convinced. That single move turns a standoff into a shared investigation.

sections.heading: Remote work needs explicit signalling
body: Without shared rooms, silence is ambiguous. Over-communicate state: what you are doing, what you finished, where you are stuck.
Document decisions where the next person will look, not where you happen to be working. A decision nobody can find is a decision that will be made again.

keyPoints: Measure teamwork by how much friction you remove for others
Hand off with goal, state, next step and risks
Critique the artifact, never the author
Say what evidence would change your mind
Write decisions where the next reader will look

examples.title: Reviewing a teammate's design
examples.body: Open with what the design gets right and why it works, then ask about the single riskiest assumption. Ask for a decision on that point before anything else changes.

examples.title: Joining an ongoing project
examples.body: Read the last two weeks of decisions first, then list what you think the project's real constraint is and ask the team to correct you. You will be productive far faster than by asking what to do.

mistakes: Going quiet when blocked because admitting it feels like failure
Rewriting a teammate's work silently instead of discussing it
Deciding in a private channel what the whole team needs to know
Treating a disagreement as a status contest rather than a technical question
practiceTip: For one week, end every work conversation by confirming who does what by when, out loud.

subject: leadership
name: Leadership & Initiative
tagline: Influence without authority
summary: Leadership is not a job title; it is the act of taking responsibility for an outcome you do not fully control. It shows up as initiative, as clarity under ambiguity, and as making the people around you more capable.

sections.heading: Initiative is a judgement call
body: Anyone can follow a ticket. Initiative is noticing the gap between what is being done and what would be valuable, then closing it without being asked.
Scale your initiative to the risk. Fixing a typo needs no permission; changing a shared interface does. Ask early for anything expensive or hard to reverse.
bullets: Notice what is nobody's job and pick up the cheap part
Propose a small experiment instead of demanding a bet
Bring a recommendation, not just a problem

sections.heading: Ownership means the outcome, not the task
body: Owners define done. They know what result matters, what could go wrong, and what the fallback is if it does. When something slips, they say so first.
Ownership also means knowing when to escalate. Carrying a blocked project alone is not loyalty, it is a hidden risk.

sections.heading: Delegate the outcome, not the steps
body: Telling someone how to do a task keeps you the bottleneck. Sharing the goal, the constraints and the definition of done lets them think.
Then be reachable for questions without hovering. Availability is support; presence becomes surveillance.

keyPoints: Notice work nobody owns and take the cheap, reversible part
Own the outcome and the definition of done, not just the task list
Escalate blockers instead of quietly absorbing them
Delegate goals and constraints, not step-by-step instructions
Bring a recommendation whenever you raise a problem

examples.title: Leading without a title
examples.body: A team keeps missing a weekly deadline. Instead of complaining, you measure the real cause, propose one process change, and run it for two weeks with the team's agreement. Initiative plus evidence.

examples.title: Escalating well
examples.body: You are blocked for a day on an external dependency. You state the blocker, the impact, the options, and your recommendation, then ask for a decision. Twenty minutes instead of three days.

mistakes: Waiting for permission for small, reversible improvements
Presenting problems without a recommendation
Escalating everything, which makes your signal worthless
Confusing activity with ownership
practiceTip: Once a week, identify one thing that is not going well, write a two-line proposal, and send it to the person who can act on it.

subject: time_management
name: Time Management & Productivity
tagline: Choose what not to do
summary: Productivity is not speed; it is spending attention on the few things that matter. Most people do not need more hours, they need fewer, better-chosen tasks and protection from the interruptions that fragment them.

sections.heading: Prioritise by consequence, not urgency
body: Urgency is a property of the clock; importance is a property of the outcome. Busy days are usually full of urgent, low-consequence work that feels productive and changes nothing.
Pick one or two things each day that would make the day worthwhile even if nothing else happened. Do those first, while attention is fresh.
bullets: Write tomorrow's one most important task before you close today
Batch shallow work into fixed windows
Finish things: a finished small task beats three open big ones

sections.heading: Protect deep work
body: Real progress needs uninterrupted blocks. Every interruption costs more than its own minutes; it costs the reload time of the context you had built.
Make focus physical: notifications off, one tab, a visible timer. If you can be interrupted in ten seconds, you will be.

sections.heading: Estimates are promises you can keep
body: Break work until the pieces are small enough to predict, then add the risk honestly. A plan with no slack is a plan with no recovery.
Say what you will drop if the deadline holds. That question surfaces the real priority faster than any status meeting.

keyPoints: Rank by consequence, not by urgency
Choose one or two tasks that define a good day
Batch shallow work; protect the blocks for deep work
Make interruption physically harder, not just discouraged
Name what will be dropped if the deadline is fixed

examples.title: A fragmented day
examples.body: Meetings, chat and review requests leave two hours before the deadline. The fix is to start the day with ninety protected minutes on the critical task, then handle the rest in batches.

examples.title: An overcommitted week
examples.body: Four things are promised for Friday. List them with consequences, move two, and tell the stakeholders which two and why. Honest triage beats silent failure on all four.

mistakes: Confusing busyness with progress
Letting notifications define the day's order
Estimating only the coding time and none of the coordination
Starting five things so none of them finish
practiceTip: Track where your time actually goes for three days before changing anything. Most people optimise the wrong block.

subject: adaptability
name: Adaptability & Learning Agility
tagline: Change your mind faster than the world changes
summary: Adaptability is the skill of updating your plans when reality disagrees with them. It combines tolerance for ambiguity, the discipline to learn from feedback, and the willingness to abandon a good idea for a better one.

sections.heading: Ambiguity is the normal state
body: Early in any project the information needed to be certain does not exist yet. Adaptive people act on the best available evidence, define what would prove them wrong, and update quickly.
Treat plans as hypotheses. The plan that never changes is usually a plan nobody is testing.
bullets: Decide what evidence would change your direction, in advance
Prefer reversible decisions early, expensive ones later
Separate what you know from what you assume

sections.heading: Feedback is data, not verdict
body: The fast learners are not the ones who are right most often; they are the ones who update fastest without ego damage. Ask for the specific observation behind the judgement.
Then check whether the feedback is about the work or about you. Keep the first, question the second, and discard neither automatically.

sections.heading: Unlearning is part of learning
body: Every new framework makes some old habits actively wrong. Spending a day discovering which of your defaults no longer apply is time well spent.
Keep a list of the beliefs you have changed. It is the most honest measure of learning you will ever keep.

keyPoints: Treat plans as hypotheses and define the disproof in advance
Act on the best available evidence; do not wait for certainty
Ask for the specific observation behind every judgement
Identify which of your old defaults the new situation breaks
Update fast and cheaply, without treating it as defeat

examples.title: A cancelled requirement
examples.body: Two weeks of work is invalidated. The adaptive response is to ask what changed, salvage the reusable pieces, and write down the assumption that failed so it is caught earlier next time.

examples.title: Harsh review feedback
examples.body: Instead of defending the design, ask which single part the reviewer would change first and why. You get a concrete, actionable item instead of a general verdict.

mistakes: Waiting for certainty before acting
Defending a plan after the evidence has turned against it
Hearing feedback as an attack on identity rather than information
Assuming last year's best practice still applies
practiceTip: After every project, write down one belief you changed. If the list is empty, you were not paying attention.

subject: conflict_resolution
name: Conflict Resolution
tagline: Disagree productively
summary: Conflict is inevitable wherever people care about outcomes. Handled well it produces better decisions; handled badly it produces politics. The skill is separating the disagreement from the relationship and finding the interest underneath the position.

sections.heading: Positions hide interests
body: A position is what someone says they want; an interest is why they want it. Two people can hold opposite positions that serve the same interest, which means there is usually a solution neither has proposed.
Ask why until you reach something that would still matter if the plan changed. That is the interest you can work with.
bullets: Ask what outcome the other person is protecting
Look for constraints both of you must respect
Name the trade-off out loud instead of arguing past it

sections.heading: De-escalate before you persuade
body: Nobody accepts a proposal from someone they feel unheard by. Lower the temperature first: acknowledge what is true in their position, then add what they are missing.
Move the conversation from blame to facts. What do we agree happened, and where exactly do our readings differ?

sections.heading: Repair the relationship afterwards
body: Disagreements leave residue even when resolved. A short private follow-up, acknowledging the friction and confirming the working relationship, clears most of it.
Never win a technical argument by making a colleague feel small. The cost shows up in every later decision.

keyPoints: Ask why until you reach the interest beneath the position
Acknowledge what is true in their view before adding yours
Move from blame to shared facts before proposing solutions
Look for constraints both sides must respect
Repair the relationship after the disagreement ends

examples.title: Two engineers, one design
examples.body: One wants speed, the other wants flexibility. Underneath, both want to avoid a painful rewrite. Naming that shared interest makes a third option visible: ship the fast version behind an interface that costs almost nothing now.

examples.title: A heated standup
examples.body: A disagreement gets personal. The recovery is a five-minute private conversation about what each person was trying to protect, followed by an agreed decision rule for next time.

mistakes: Arguing positions instead of exploring interests
Escalating to a manager as the first move
Winning the point and losing the working relationship
Letting a resolved disagreement stay unresolved personally
practiceTip: In your next disagreement, write one sentence describing the other side's case so well they would agree you understood it.

subject: emotional_intelligence
name: Emotional Intelligence
tagline: Read the room, then manage yourself
summary: Emotional intelligence is the ability to notice emotions accurately, in yourself and in others, and to use that information deliberately. In technical work it shows up as composure under pressure and as reading a room before acting in it.

sections.heading: Self-awareness comes first
body: You cannot manage a state you have not noticed. Learn your own signals: the moment your writing gets clipped, when you start re-reading the same paragraph, when you need to leave the room.
Name the state to yourself without judgement. Labelling an emotion measurably reduces its grip, which is why the pause works.
bullets: Track your early warning signs of stress
Separate the trigger from your interpretation of it
Use a deliberate pause before responding when activated

sections.heading: Empathy is a hypothesis
body: You cannot read minds, but you can form a hypothesis about what someone is experiencing and check it. That is far better than assuming they share your context.
Empathy does not mean agreement. It means accounting for the other person's reality when you decide how to act.

sections.heading: Regulation is a skill, not a personality
body: Composure is a practice, like any other. Sleep, breaks and boundaries are not soft; they are the inputs that determine whether you can regulate at all.
When you cannot regulate, say so plainly and step back. Announcing your state is always allowed, and usually respected.

keyPoints: Learn your own early warning signs of stress
Name the state without judgement before acting
Treat your read of someone's emotion as a hypothesis to check
Empathy means accounting for their reality, not agreeing with it
Say your state out loud when you cannot regulate it

examples.title: A tense code review
examples.body: You notice your replies getting shorter. Instead of sending one more comment, you write that you will return after a break, then re-read the thread and ask a question instead of asserting.

examples.title: A frustrated teammate
examples.body: Rather than solving immediately, you say what you think they are frustrated about and ask whether that is right. Being understood usually lowers the temperature more than a fix does.

mistakes: Treating a bad day as a permanent verdict about a person
Confusing empathy with agreement
Suppressing emotions until they leak out sideways
Ignoring the physical inputs that make regulation possible
practiceTip: Keep a one-line note of what activated you each day for a week. Patterns show up faster than you expect.

subject: workplace_ethics
name: Workplace Ethics & Professionalism
tagline: Behave the same when nobody is watching
summary: Professional ethics is the set of defaults you apply when nobody is watching and no rule is written. Trust is built from small, consistent choices and destroyed by a single visible compromise.

sections.heading: Integrity is a habit, not a dilemma
body: Most ethical failures are not dramatic decisions; they are small conveniences taken once and then repeated. The honest estimate, the credit given properly, the data not quietly excluded.
Decide your defaults in advance for the situations you will actually meet, so the decision is made calmly rather than under pressure.
bullets: Give credit specifically and publicly; take it rarely
Report the number you measured, including the bad ones
Disclose conflicts of interest before they are discovered

sections.heading: Boundaries protect both sides
body: Respect for other people's time, attention and personal information is a professional skill. Silence about a colleague's private matters is part of the job.
Saying no to unreasonable requests is also ethical: quietly accepting work you cannot do well misleads everyone who depends on you.

sections.heading: Escalate early, in the right channel
body: If you see something unsafe, dishonest or illegal, raise it through the defined channel while it is small. Early reporting is almost always treated as diligence rather than trouble.
Document what you observed, not what you concluded. Facts survive scrutiny; inferences do not.

keyPoints: Decide your defaults in advance, not under pressure
Report the measurement, including the inconvenient numbers
Give specific public credit; keep confidential matters confidential
Disclose conflicts before someone else finds them
Escalate early with observations, not conclusions

examples.title: A tempting shortcut
examples.body: A test can be skipped to hit a release date. The professional move is to state the risk clearly, in writing, and let the decision be made by someone accountable for it.

examples.title: Credit for shared work
examples.body: A demo goes well and everyone thanks you. You name the three people whose work actually made it possible, specifically. Trust compounds from exactly this.

mistakes: Taking quiet credit for shared work
Hiding a bad metric instead of explaining it
Treating confidentiality as optional once a secret is boring
Accepting work you cannot deliver to avoid a difficult conversation
practiceTip: Before each commitment, ask whether you would be comfortable if it appeared in a public document with your name on it.

subject: career_planning
name: Career Planning & Growth
tagline: Build the next role before you need it
summary: Careers are built from deliberate compounding, not from occasional lucky breaks. The people who move fastest are usually the ones who chose a direction early, collected the right kind of evidence, and made their work visible.

sections.heading: Choose a direction, then test it
body: A generalist drift feels safe and is hard to explain. Pick a direction you can defend, and collect evidence: projects, shipped work, measurable outcomes.
Directions are hypotheses too. Revisit them once or twice a year with honest evidence, not anxiety.
bullets: Name the role you want in two years and the gap to it
Prefer projects that produce visible evidence
Track outcomes, not hours or effort

sections.heading: Networking is maintenance, not promotion
body: The strongest networks are built before you need them, by being useful without expectation. A short message that helps someone is worth more than a hundred connection requests.
Keep in touch with people you worked well with. Most good roles are filled by someone who was already known.

sections.heading: Interviews are demonstrations, not quizzes
body: An interview is a sample of how you think and work together. Narrate your reasoning, ask clarifying questions, and treat it as a collaboration rather than an exam.
Prepare evidence for the claims on your CV: what you did, what changed, what you learned. The story matters more than the technology list.

keyPoints: Choose a direction you can defend, and revisit it with evidence
Collect visible evidence: shipped work and outcomes
Be useful to your network before you need it
Narrate your reasoning during interviews; treat them as collaboration
Track outcomes rather than effort

examples.title: Preparing for a target role
examples.body: You want to move into platform work. You take the internal migration nobody wanted, cut deployment time measurably, and write it up. That is an interview answer before the interview.

examples.title: A stalled application
examples.body: Instead of re-applying to the same postings, you ask two people in the field what their teams struggle with, then build one small thing that helps. Visibility beats volume.

mistakes: Drifting as a generalist with no defensible story
Networking only when job hunting
Listing technologies instead of outcomes
Treating an interview as an exam to pass rather than a collaboration
practiceTip: Every quarter, write one paragraph describing what you can now do that you could not do a year ago.

subject: presentation
name: Presentation & Storytelling
tagline: One slide, one idea, one story
summary: A presentation is not a document read aloud; it is a guided experience with a beginning, a turn and a landing. Structure and narrative do more for comprehension than polish or slides ever will.

sections.heading: Structure carries the audience
body: Open with the situation, name the problem or opportunity, then the resolution. Audiences forgive plain slides; they do not forgive losing the thread.
One idea per slide. If a slide needs two titles, it needs to be two slides.
bullets: State the takeaway in the first thirty seconds
Build slides from the talk, not the talk from the slides
Rehearse the transitions, which is where talks break

sections.heading: Story beats summary
body: People remember narrative. A concrete problem, a real obstacle and a resolution land further than an abstraction list.
Use specifics deliberately: a number, a person, a moment. They anchor the abstract claim you are making.

sections.heading: Delivery is mostly preparation
body: Nerves are normal and mostly disappear once you are speaking. The fix is preparation, not confidence: know your first two sentences cold and have a clear landing.
Handle questions by repeating them, then answering the question asked. If you do not know, say so and follow up in writing.

keyPoints: Open with situation, problem and resolution
One idea per slide; the talk drives the slides
Use concrete specifics to anchor abstract claims
Know your opening and your closing cold
Repeat the question, then answer what was asked

examples.title: A technical talk that landed
examples.body: Instead of listing features, the speaker opened with the incident that motivated the work, showed the two minutes of chaos, then the fix. The feature list arrived as evidence, not as the point.

examples.title: A design review
examples.body: One slide per decision, each with the option chosen, the alternative rejected and the reason. Reviewers can argue with a decision instead of decoding a diagram.

mistakes: Reading dense slides aloud
Burying the takeaway at the end of a data dump
Skipping rehearsal because the content is familiar
Answering a different question than the one asked
practiceTip: Give your next five-minute talk to one colleague first. The questions they ask are the questions your audience will ask.
